t:
Select the grammatically correct sentence.
A. As a nation, India is a united country and shall always remain so.
B.As nation, India is a united country and shall always remain so.
C.As the nation, India is a united country and shall always remain so.
D.As a nation, India is an united country and shall always remain so.
e: The grammatically correct sentence is A. This sentence is coherent and use the right articles. Sentence B is incorrect due to the omission of the article "a" before the noun "nation." It should be "As a nation" to indicate that India is being referred to as one of many nations. Without the article, the sentence lacks proper grammar. Sentence C is incorrect because it adds the definite article "the" before "nation". The use of "the" implies that there is a specific or particular nation being referred to, rather than India being considered as one among many nations. Using the definite article "the" before "nation" would not accurately convey the intended meaning of the sentence, which is to highlight India as a nation in general. Instead, the indefinite article "a" is more appropriate in this context to indicate that India is being considered as one among many nations. Sentence D is incorrect because of the use of the indefinite article "an" before "united country." The correct form should use "a" instead of "an." "A" is used before words that begin with a consonant sound, while "an" is used before words that begin with a vowel sound. In the given case, the word "united" starts with a consonant sound. Accordingly, article "a" should be used. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. NOTE: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. He attended a event. The event was an important one.
B. He attended an event. A event was important.
C. He attended an event. The event was important.
D. He attended a event. An event was important.
e: Option A: Incorrect. The indefinite article 'a' is incorrectly used before "event," which starts with a vowel sound, requiring 'an' as "an" is used before vowel-sounding words, while "a" is used before consonant-sounding words. The second sentence correctly uses 'the event' but cannot compensate for the first error. Option B: Incorrect. 'An event' is correct in the first sentence, but 'A event' in the second sentence is incorrect for the same reason as above. Option C: Correct. Both sentences use the correct articles: 'an event' for the first sentence and 'the event' for the specific event referenced in the second sentence. Option D: Incorrect. The first sentence repeats the error of using 'a event'. The second sentence is also incorrect because "an" fails to denote specificity. Hence, option (b) is the answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: a most remarkable series of inscriptions
buried deep within the cavern’s walls.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (D) 👉 No replacement required. 📌 Rule / Concept: The Use of "A Most" the superlative word "most" is usually preceded by the definite article the when it is used to compare three or more things (e.g., "the most beautiful city in the world"). However, "most" can also be used as an adverb meaning "very" or "exceedingly." When "most" is used in this sense to provide emphasis rather than to make a direct comparison, it is preceded by the indefinite article a. [ In short; A MOST = VERY ] 💢 Application to the Given Question (a most remarkable series of inscriptions) In this sentence, the speaker is not comparing these inscriptions to all other inscriptions in the world to find a "winner." Instead, they are simply stating that the inscriptions were very remarkable. Therefore, "a most" is grammatically correct and appropriate for the context. Corrected Sentence The archaeological survey team discovered a most remarkable series of inscriptions buried deep within the cavern’s walls. ✅ More Examples for Clarity Example 1 This is a most interesting story you have shared with us. (Meaning: a very interesting story) ✅ Example 2 Mr. Khanna is a most diligent employee. (Meaning: a very diligent employee) ✅ ❌ Incorrect Usage Wrong example 1 He is the most kind man I met yesterday. (Unless comparing him to all men ever met, use "a most" for "a very"). ❌ Wrong example 2 It was a most tallest building in the city. ("Most" cannot be used with an "-est" adjective; this is a double superlative error). ❌ 🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips Comparison vs. Description: If the sentence ends with a comparison group (e.g., "in the class," "of the two," "in the world"), use The Most. If it is just a descriptive statement of quality, A Most is often the intended "trappy" correct answer. The "Very" Test: If you can replace "most" with "very" and the sentence makes perfect sense without needing a comparison, "A Most" is correct.

t:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. Identify the part that has an error. Select 'No error' if there is no error. 
Hide treats inside <u>an empty cardboard egg</u> carton <u>to challenge they</u> to learn <u>how to open the box</u>.
e: Option d): This part contains the error. The word "they" is a subjective pronoun, which cannot be used in this context because it follows the verb "challenge." We need an objective pronoun as the object of the verb "challenge". The correct objective pronoun should be "them." Thus, it should read "to challenge them." So, replace "they" with "them" to rectify the error. The correct sentence is: Hide treats inside an empty cardboard egg carton to challenge them to learn how to open the box. Hence, option (d) is the answer. Note: Subjective Pronouns: The pronouns I, you, we, he, she, it, and they are known as subjective pronouns because they act as the subjects of verbs: We went to the party. Objective Pronouns: The pronouns me, you, us, him, her, it, and them are called objective pronouns because they act as the objects of verbs and prepositions: Anjali drove us home.

t:
The following sentence has been split into three segments. Identify the segment that contains an error. If the sentence is free of any errors, mark 'No error' as your answer. 
This is the same painting which adorned/ the walls of our ancestral home, / evoking nostalgic memories of bygone eras.
o: this is the same painting which adorned
the walls of our ancestral home
evoking nostalgic memories of bygone eras
e: All, any, the only, the same, none, much, the little, the few, something, anything, nothing and superlative degrees are all followed by 'that' only. They cannot be followed by 'who' or 'which'. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. The corrected sentence: This is the same painting that adorned the walls of our ancestral home, evoking nostalgic memories of bygone eras. Note: · The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made. · The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared. · The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
She is looking forward to meet / her old school friends again / at the upcoming alumni event.
o: She is looking forward to meet
e: The error is in the part "She is looking forward to meet". The phrase 'look forward to' is a phrasal verb. When a verb follows this phrase, it must be in the gerund form (verb + -ing). The 'to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition, not an infinitive marker. Prepositions are followed by nouns or gerunds. Therefore, the infinitive 'meet' should be replaced by the gerund 'meeting'. Correct Sentence: She is looking forward to meeting her old school friends again at the upcoming alumni event. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. Note: · Phrasal verb: A phrase that consists of a verb with a preposition or adverb or both, the meaning of which is different from the meaning of its separate parts. Example: She has always looked down on me. Here, the phrasal verb 'to look down on someone' doesn't mean that you are looking down from a higher place at someone who is below you; it means that you think that you are better than someone. · Gerund: Gerund is a verb form that functions as a noun, ending in -ing. A gerund can be either the subject or object of a sentence in English. Example: "Everybody enjoyed her dancing and singing at the party." The words 'dancing' and 'singing' are gerunds.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
When Sanathan asked Mr. Jignesh / for a fresh evaluation of his performance / in the last financial year, / little did him know that the results will come out worse than expected.
o: for a fresh evaluation of his performance
little did him know that the results will come out worse than expected
e: The sentence contains a pronoun error. The objective pronoun 'him' should be replaced with its subjective pronoun 'he' as the verb 'know' requires a subject. Therefore, the error is in the part in option (d). The correct sentence is: When Sanathan asked Mr. Jignesh for a fresh evaluation of his performance in the last financial year, little did he know that the results will come out worse than expected. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer. Note: Objective Pronouns: The pronouns me, you, us, him, her, it, and them are called objective pronouns because they act as the objects of verbs and prepositions: Anjali drove us home. Subjective Pronouns: The pronouns I, you, we, he, she, it, and they are known as subjective pronouns because they act as the subjects of verbs: We went to the party.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Had he worked a little harder, / he would have certainly succeeded / in the final examination last year.
o: Had he worked a little harder
in the final examination last year
e: The given sentence is grammatically correct and contains no error. It is a Type 3 conditional sentence, used for expressing a hypothetical situation in the past that did not happen. The standard structure is "If + Past Perfect, ... would have + V3". This sentence uses the inverted form where 'If' is omitted and the auxiliary verb 'had' is placed before the subject ('Had he worked...'). This is a correct and advanced grammatical structure. Correct Sentence: Had he worked a little harder, he would have certainly succeeded in the final examination last year. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. Recently, an documentary on Cold War was screened. It provided the comprehensive overview of that period.
B. Recently, the documentary on a Cold War was screened. It provided a comprehensive overview of that period.
C. Recently, a documentary on an Cold War was screened. It provided an comprehensive overview of that period.
D. Recently, a documentary on the Cold War was screened. It provided a comprehensive overview of period.
e: The indefinite article 'a' should be used before 'documentary' because it is introducing an unspecified noun 'documentary'. Similarly, the indefinite article 'a' should also be used before 'comprehensive' because it refers to an unspecified and singular noun, that is, 'overview'. Also, since 'documentary' and 'comprehensive' are not vowel-sounding words, they cannot be preceded by 'an'. The definite article 'the' should be used before 'Cold War' because it introduces a specific noun 'Cold War'. No indefinite article is used before 'overview' because it is uncountable in nature. The sentences A, B, and C depict grammatically incorrect usage of the articles. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
I had walked / for most of the day / to Kanpur and then / get on the train by Mumbai.
o: Get on the train by Mumbai
e: The sentence contains a prepositional error. The phrase 'get on the train by Mumbai' is incorrect. The sentence talks about the journey to someplace. We cannot use the preposition 'by' before the destination. The preposition 'to' can be used to indicate the destination of the journey. For example: Let's all go to the cinema tonight! We can use 'by' to indicate the mode of transport. For example: We went to Pisa by train. Also, since the sentence denotes two actions done in past, one after another, 'get' should be replaced with the past tense form 'got'. The correct sentence is- 'I had walked for most of the day to Kanpur and then got on the train to Mumbai.' Hence, option (c) is the correct answer. Note: A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples I. The teacher scolded the child for being late. II. We're going to a party. · The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition. · The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Having found a two thousand / rupee note, both kids went / to their father to / divide it among them.
e: The preposition 'between' is used when we talk about two persons or things. Example: Between red and yellow, I will prefer red. The preposition 'among' is used when we talk about more than two persons or things. Example: Please choose one among the five options. In the given sentence, two thousand rupees are to be divided between two kids (as indicated by the determiner 'both'). So, 'among' in the sentence should be replaced with 'between' to rectify the error. So, there is an error in option d). Hence, option d) is correct.

t: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
o: Ragini plays the guitar with a melody.
Ragini plays the guitar with melodiousness.
e:
· Option 1: "Ragini plays the guitar melodiously" uses "melodiously" (an adverb) to modify "plays," correctly describing how she plays. This is grammatically correct.
· Option 2: "Ragini plays the guitar melodious" uses "melodious" (an adjective) instead of an adverb, which is incorrect as it cannot modify the verb "plays."
· Option 3: "Ragini plays the guitar with a melody" is grammatically correct but changes the meaning slightly; it suggests she plays a specific tune rather than describing her playing style.
· Option 4: "Ragini plays the guitar with melodiousness" uses "melodiousness" (a noun) with "with," which is awkward and less natural than an adverb.
Option 1 is the most straightforward and grammatically correct choice, making it the answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The Aryans utilized swift horses in
their military campaigns that was the
primary reason for their tactical superiority.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B)Replace “that” with “which”.Rule / Concept: Relative Pronouns Referring to a Clause -In English grammar, when we want a relative pronoun to refer back to an entire preceding idea or a whole clause (rather than just the noun immediately before it), we must use "which." The relative pronoun "that" cannot be used to refer to a whole sentence or statement; it can only refer to a specific noun or pronoun (the antecedent).Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, what was the primary reason for their superiority? It wasn't just the "campaigns" (plural) themselves. It was the entire fact/action mentioned in the first part of the sentence: "The Aryans utilized swift horses in their military campaigns." Since the relative pronoun is referring to this entire statement as a single reason, "that" is incorrect. It must be replaced with "which."More Examples for ClarityExample 1 ✅: He passed the exam with flying colors, which surprised everyone. (The fact that he passed surprised them).Example 2 ✅: It rained all day, which ruined our plans for the picnic. (The fact that it rained ruined the plans).Example 3 ✅: She ignored my advice, which was a very foolish thing to do. (The act of ignoring advice was foolish).

t:
Select the grammatically correct sentence. 
A) They decided to starts a small business together. They have already secured a location and are preparing for their grand opening.
B) They decided to started a small business together. They have already secured a location and are preparing for their grand opening.
C) They decided to started a small business together. They have already secured a location and are preparing for there grand opening.
D) They decided to start a small business together. They have already secured a location and are preparing for their grand opening.
e: The grammatically correct sentence is D. After the infinitive marker "to", we usually use the base form of the verb. So, the correct base form to use after 'to' is 'start' (used in D). 'Starts' (used in A) is the present tense form, not the base form of the verb. 'Started' (used in B and C) is the past tense form, not the base form of the verb. Also, in sentence C, "there" should be replaced with "their." "There" is used to refer to a place, while "their" is the possessive form that is needed to indicate that the grand opening belongs to "them." Hence, (a) is the correct answer. NOTE: "Infinitive: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, often preceded by to. Consider the sentences given below: · To err is human. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to err' is the subject of the verb 'is'] · My father likes to cook. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to cook' is the object of the verb 'likes'] · To vote in elections is our right. [the infinitive 'to vote', like a noun, is the subject of the verb 'is', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (elections)] · Radha went to the lake to fetch water. [the infinitive 'to fetch', like a noun, is the object of the verb 'went', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (water)] · The above sentences illustrate various ways in which infinitives are used. It can both act as a noun and a verb."

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Despite several rounds of intense deliberations with the international trade
commission, the federal government has still to announce the
comprehensive new tax regulations for the upcoming fiscal year.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “has still to announce” with “has yet to announce”. Rule / Concept: Still vs. Yet Still: Used for an action that is continuing (It began in the past and is happening now). It usually goes before the main verb or after the "be" verb. Yet: Used for an action that is expected to happen but hasn't happened. It usually goes at the end of a sentence. Application to the Given Question "...the federal government has still to announce the comprehensive new tax regulations..." In this sentence, the structure used is Subject + Has + [Adverb] + Infinitive (to announce). This specific setup describes a pending action. Grammatically, "still" is incorrect here because "still" describes continuity, whereas "yet" describes something that remains undone. The fixed idiomatic expression for a pending official action is always "has yet to". Corrected Sentence Despite several rounds of intense deliberations with the international trade commission, the federal government has yet to announce the comprehensive new tax regulations for the upcoming fiscal year. More Examples for Clarity Example 1: The results have yet to be declared. ✅ Example 2: He is still waiting for the bus. (Continuity) ✅ Example 3: I haven't received the mail yet. (Expected action at the end) ✅ Incorrect Usage Wrong example 1: We have still to decide the winner. (Should be have yet to) ✅ Wrong example 2: Is it yet raining outside? (Should be still raining) ✅

t: Which one of the following is a correct sentence?
o: Our marketing endeavours focus in building a deep emotional connection while creating an appreciation for platinum's unique qualities.
Our marketing endeavours focuses on building a deep emotional connection while creating an appreciation for platinum's unique qualities.
Our marketing endeavours focus on building a deep emotional connection since creating an appreciation for platinum's unique qualities.
Our marketing endeavours focus on building a deep emotional connection while creating an appreciation for platinum's unique qualities.
e: The correct answer is option (d) as it maintains a clear and coherent structure in expressing the focus of marketing endeavours. Let us look at the incorrect options: Option (a): The preposition "in" is incorrect; it should be "focus on building." Therefore, this option has a preposition error. Option (b): There is a subject-verb agreement error in this option. The plural subject "Our marketing endeavours" should take the plural verb "focus," not the singular verb "focuses." Option (c): The use of "since" is not suitable in this context. "Since" is used to express a cause or reason, but it doesn't appropriately connect the ideas in the sentence. Any conjunction like "while" is more fitting for expressing simultaneous actions.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. 
I think that he must have fall upon some bushes and vines that grew in some parts of the chasm.
e: The verbs 'has, have, had' are followed by past participles when the sentence is in active voice. So, the use of 'fall' is incorrect. The correct sentence is- I think that he must have fallen upon some bushes and vines that grew in some parts of the chasm. Hence, option (a) is correct.

t:
Spot the error in the given sentence and select the correct sentence from the options given.
She likes to made people lose their cool by starting belligerent political arguments.
o: She likes to makes people lose their cool by starting belligerent political arguments.
She likes to making people lose their cool by starting belligerent political arguments.
She likes to be make people lose their cool by starting belligerent political arguments.
She likes to make people lose their cool by starting belligerent political arguments.
e: The infinitive marker 'To' is always followed by a base form of the verb, so the use of 'made/makes/making' [V2/V3, V5, V4 respectively] will be incorrect here. 'To + be' is followed by a participle form of the verb which is not the case in option (c) ['make' is the base verb], therefore, it will be incorrect as well. The grammatically correct sentence is mentioned in option (d). The correct sentence is - 'She likes to make people lose their cool by starting belligerent political arguments.' Hence, option (d) is correct. NOTE/- Infinitive marker: A word or affix attached to the stem of a verb in order to form the full infinitive. In English, to is the infinitive marker. Infinitive: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, often preceded by to. Consider the sentences given below: · To err is human. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to err' is the subject of the verb 'is'] · My father likes to cook. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to cook' is the object of the verb 'likes'] · To vote in elections is our right. [the infinitive 'to vote', like a noun, is the subject of the verb 'is', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (elections)] · Radha went to the lake to fetch water. [the infinitive 'to fetch', like a noun, is the object of the verb 'went', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (water)] · The above sentences illustrate various ways in which infinitives are used. It can both act as a noun and a verb. Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

t:
In the following question, a sentence is given which is divided into four parts. Out of the four parts, one part contains an error. Mark that option as your answer. 
A number of activities (A)/ including the sale of essential goods is (B)/ relaxed during the (C)/ lockdown period by the government. (D)
e:
Part B has an error. 
The phrase 'a number of' takes a plural noun and a plural verb after it. The phrase, 'the number of' takes a plural noun but a singular verb after it.
Therefore, in the given sentence, the singular auxiliary verb 'is' should be replaced with its plural form 'are' to rectify the given sentence. 
Hence, option (c) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: A number of activities including the sale of essential goods are relaxed during the lockdown period by the government.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The manager asked / the cooking team, "Who / among you is to baked the / Christmas cake this year?"
o: among you is to baked the
e: The segment "among you is to baked the" contains a grammatical error. The verb "baked" is incorrect in this context; it should be "bake" to maintain the infinitive form after the phrase "is to." The correct construction would be "among you is to bake the." The other segments are grammatically correct: "The manager asked" is a valid introductory clause, "the cooking team, 'Who'" is part of a direct question, and "Christmas cake this year?" completes the question appropriately. t: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
o: The company has invested a large amount of money in new machineries.
The company has invested a large amount of money in new machinery.
The company has invested a large number of money in new machinery.
The company has invested a large number of money in new machineries.
e: The correct answer is option b). Explanation: "Machinery" is an uncountable noun and hence, cannot have a plural form. So, "machineries" is incorrect. This makes options a) and d) incorrect. Additionally, "amount" is used with uncountable nouns like "money," while "number" is used with countable nouns. This makes option c) incorrect. Note: Countable and uncountable nouns: 1. Countable nouns are the class of nouns that can be counted, for example, 'table' - one table, two tables, three tables, etc. 2. Uncountable nouns are the nouns that cannot be counted or usually are not counted, for example, light, water, milk, information, furniture, etc. They do not generally have a plural form and can't be preceded by 'a' or 'an'. Many abstract nouns are typically uncountable. Some uncountable nouns can be used in the plural as well, depending on the meaning or context of the word.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error. 
By the time the event ended, she had give a heartfelt speech that moved everyone in the audience to tears.
o: By the time the event ended,
she had give a heartfelt speech
e: In segment (b), "she had give" is incorrect. The correct past participle form of the verb "give" is "given." When using the past perfect tense ("had given"), we need to use the past participle form of the verb. Therefore, "had give" should be corrected to "had given" to maintain grammatical accuracy in the sentence. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. Note: A past participle is a verb form that typically ends in "-ed" for regular verbs and has various endings for irregular verbs. It is used in forming perfect tenses, passive voice, and as an adjective to describe nouns. The corrected sentence: By the time the event ended, she had given a heartfelt speech that moved everyone in the audience to tears.

t:
There is an error in the given sentence. From the options given, identify the sentence that corrects the error to make it a grammatically accurate sentence.
Harmit is not innocent such as Uday.
o: Harmit is not as innocent more than Uday.
Harmit is not as much as innocent as Uday.
Harmit is not as innocent as Uday.
Harmit is not innocent than Uday.
e: When making comparisons in English, the correct structure for negative comparisons is "not as + adjective + as." The original sentence incorrectly uses "such as," which is used to introduce examples, not for comparison. Option 3 correctly uses "not as innocent as" to properly compare Harmit's innocence to Uday's.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Although the mountaineer was very weak, / he was determined to reach the summit / without nobody's assistance.
o: he was determined to reach the summit
Although the mountaineer was very weak
e: The error is in the part "without nobody's assistance". This creates a double negative, which is grammatically incorrect in standard English. 'Without' is a negative preposition, and 'nobody's' is a negative pronoun. Using two negatives in the same clause makes the meaning positive (e.g., 'not having no help' would logically mean 'having some help'), which contradicts the intended meaning. To correct this, one of the negatives should be replaced with a positive equivalent. We can either say 'with nobody's assistance' or 'without anybody's assistance'. The latter is more suitable here. Correct Sentence: Although the mountaineer was very weak, he was determined to reach the summit without anybody's assistance. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The company introduced two comprehensive policies this year after extensive consultation with department heads and employee representatives: one on leave
management, which aims to simplify the process of availing leaves, and the other on performance appraisal, which focuses on evaluating employees fairly
and systematically; the later, which was drafted after careful analysis of previous appraisal challenges, aims to reward deserving employees more effectively
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) – Replace “later” with “latter”.Rule / Concept: Later vs. LatterLater → Refers to time (afterward, afterwards).Latter → Refers to the second of two things mentioned.Trap: In SSC CGL long sentences, candidates often use “later” when referring to the second item instead of “latter”.Application to the Given Question - Here, “the later” is incorrectly used. It refers to the second policy, performance appraisal, so the correct word is “the latter”.More Examples for Clarity -I bought two books: one on history and the other on economics; the latter is more interesting. The team analyzed two strategies: one for marketing and the other for operations; the latter proved more effective. Two candidates were shortlisted: Ankit and Ravi; the latter will be interviewed first. Incorrect Usage -I met two candidates; the later will be interviewed first. The company introduced two policies; the later focuses on appraisal. Things to Remember / Exam Tips -Check if the word refers to time (later) or the second of two things (latter).SSC CGL traps often appear in long sentences with semicolons or multiple clauses.

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. An unexpected act of kindness can strengthen our relationships. It can be practised through an acts of generosity and empathy.
B. A unexpected act of kindness can strengthen our relationships. It can be practised through the acts of generosity and empathy.
C. An unexpected act of kindness can strengthen our relationships. It can be practised through acts of generosity and empathy.
D. The unexpected act of kindness can strengthen our relationships. It can be practised through a acts of generosity and empathy.
e: The indefinite article 'an' should be used before 'unexpected' primarily because it has a vowel sound. Also, 'an' is referring to an unspecified noun in the sentence, that is, 'act'. None of the articles is used before the noun 'acts' in the second sentence because it is a plural and unspecified noun. The sentences A, B, and D depict grammatically incorrect usage of the articles. Hence, (d) is the correct answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t:
Select the grammatically correct sentence. 

A. Fruits are a good source of vitamins. An healthy diet should include fruits.
B. Fruits are an good source of vitamins. A healthy diet should include fruits.
C. Fruits are a good source of vitamins. A healthy diet should include fruits.
D. Fruits are an good source of vitamins. An healthy diet should include fruits.
e: Sentence C is grammatically correct. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. A - "An healthy" is incorrect because the indefinite article "an" is used before words starting with a vowel sound. "Healthy" starts with a consonant sound, so the definite article "a" should be used instead. B- "An good" is incorrect because the indefinite article "an" is used before words starting with a vowel sound. "Good" starts with a consonant sound, so the definite article "a" should be used instead. D- Both "an good" and "an healthy" are incorrect for the reasons mentioned above. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Provided that the weather will remain
clear tomorrow morning, the hikers will
attempt to reach the summit of the peak.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “will remain” with “remains”. 📌 Rule / Concept: The Conditional Clause Restriction In a First Conditional sentence (which talks about real or possible future events), the sentence is divided into two parts: The Condition (The "If/Provided that" part): Must be in Simple Present Tense (V1/V{s/es}). The Result (The "Will" part): Must be in Simple Future Tense (will + V1). Even though the "weather remaining clear" is something that will happen in the future, the conjunction "Provided that" (which works just like "If") locks the verb into the Present Tense. 💢 Application to the Question "Provided that the weather will remain clear tomorrow... the hikers will attempt..." The Error: Using "will" twice. You cannot have "will" in the conditional clause and the main clause simultaneously. The Logic: The condition "weather remains clear" is treated as a present requirement for the future action "will attempt" to happen. The Subject: Since "the weather" is an uncountable/singular noun, we use the singular verb form "remains." Corrected Sentence Provided that the weather remains clear tomorrow morning, the hikers will attempt to reach the summit of the peak. 🧠 Exam Tip: The "Future Conjunction" List Whenever you see these words, scan the verb immediately following them. If it has a "will" or "shall," it's almost certainly an error: If / Provided that / Supposing When / As soon as / Before / After Until / Unless / In case

t:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
A company can / make money by / obtain resources / more affordably.
e:
The error lies in the segment "obtain resources." When the preposition "by" is followed by a verb to indicate the means of achieving something, the verb should be in the gerund form (verb + -ing). The correct phrase is "obtaining resources," as the gerund is required after "by."
· Option 1 ("A company can") is correct as the subject and modal verb.
· Option 2 ("make money by") is correct, setting up the gerund requirement.
· Option 3 ("obtain resources") should be "obtaining resources."
· Option 4 ("more affordably") is correct as a comparative adverb.
Thus, the segment with the error is obtain resources.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The chef cooked the meal perfectly, / but the new soup tasted / very bitterly to all the guests.
o: The chef cooked the meal perfectly
very bitterly to all the guests
e: The error is in the part "very bitterly to all the guests". The verb 'tasted' is a verb of sensation (like feel, seem, appear, smell, sound). Such verbs are followed by an adjective that describes the quality of the subject, not an adverb. Here, 'bitterly' is an adverb modifying the action of tasting, which is incorrect. We need an adjective to describe the soup itself. The correct word to use is the adjective 'bitter'. Correct Sentence: The chef cooked the meal perfectly, but the new soup tasted very bitter to all the guests. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If the sentence is error-free, mark 'No error' as the answer.
The painting is most unique and (A)/ one-of-a-kind, with (B)/ no other copies or (C)/ replicas in existence. (D)
e: The adjectives - empty, excellent, circular, extreme, chief, entire, complete, perfect, final, last, unique, universal, round, square, triangular, eternal, etc. are not used in the comparative or superlative degree. So, 'most' should be removed from part A. The correct sentence is- The painting is unique and one-of-a-kind, with no other copies or replicas in existence. Hence, option (a) is correct.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: to find that a wolf had
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C). Replace “slayed” with “slain”.📌 Rule / Concept: Irregular Verb Forms (Slay) The verb Slay means to kill violently.Base Form (V1): SlayPast Tense (V2): SlewPast Participle (V3): Slain💢 Application to the Given Question - The sentence uses the Past Perfect tense indicated by the auxiliary verb "had". This requires the Past Participle (V3) form of the verb. Following the formal rule, the V3 of slay is slain, not "slayed." Even though "slayed" might sound acceptable in a modern conversational context, it is marked as a grammatical error in high-level exam standards.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: As per the newly updated safety regulations introduced
by the government, only vaccinating employees
are allowed to enter the corporate building.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “vaccinating” with “vaccinated”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Present Participle (V{ing}) vs. Past Participle (V3) Participles act as adjectives to describe a noun. Choosing between the -ing and the -ed/V3 form depends on whether the noun is the doer (Active) or the receiver (Passive) of the action. Present Participle (V{ing}): Used when the noun performs the action. Example: A crying baby (The baby is doing the crying). Past Participle (V3): Used when the noun receives the action or is in a particular state because of the action. Example: A broken vase (The vase received the action of breaking). 💢 Application to the Given Question "...only vaccinating employees are allowed to enter..." In this sentence, the word "employees" is the noun being described. If we say "vaccinating employees," it means the employees are currently giving vaccines to other people (like doctors or nurses). If we say "vaccinated employees," it means the employees have received the vaccine themselves. Since the safety regulation is about who is protected against the virus to enter a building, we need the passive form. The employees received the vaccine; therefore, they are vaccinated. Corrected Sentence As per the newly updated safety regulations introduced by the government, only vaccinated employees are allowed to enter the corporate building.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains an error.
(A) It is sad / (B) that you / (C) are believing / (D) in superstitious rituals.
e:
The error lies in part 3 "are believing." The verb "believe" is a stative verb, which describes a state rather than an action. Stative verbs are generally not used in continuous tenses like "are believing." The correct form should be "believe." 
The correct sentence: It is sad that you believe in superstitious rituals.
Hence, the correct answer is option 2.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The heavy rainfall caused the river to
overflow its banks, and the surrounding
fields were completely overflown by dawn.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C). Replace “overflown” with “overflowed”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Confusing Verb Forms (Fly vs. Flow) - This is a high-level trap involving two verbs that seem similar in their past participle forms but have entirely different meanings:1. Flow (to move like a liquid): The forms are Flow — Flowed — Flowed.2. Fly (to move through the air): The forms are Fly — Flew — Flown.When a river exceeds its limits, we are talking about the movement of water (Flow). Therefore, past participle must be overflowed. "Overflown" would imply the river was flying over its banks like an airplane.💢 Application to the Given Question - In the context of a river and heavy rainfall, the intended meaning is that the water "flowed over" the fields. As established, the V3 (past participle) of Flow is Flowed. Using Overflown is a grammatical error because that word is specifically reserved for the verb Fly.More Examples for Clarity - Example 1: The milk has overflowed the pan because you left the heat too high.Example 2: The pilot has flown this route more than a hundred times.Example 3: Information has flowed freely since the new policy was implemented.🧠 Things to Remember / Exam TipsLiquid = Flowed: If it involves water, sewage, or even "cash flow," the ending is always -ed.Wings = Flown: If it involves birds, planes, or time (Time flies!), use Flown.The SSC Favorite: This is a top-tier "Mains" level error because "overflown" sounds correct to the untrained ear. Always double-check the "root" verb (Is it Flow or Fly?).

t:
Identify the error in the tense of the sentence and select the option that correctly rectifies the error.
Between two evils, I always picks the one I have never tried before.
o: Between two evils, I always pick the one I have never tried before.
Between two evils, I always is picking the one I have never tried before.
Between two evils, I always picked the one I have never tried before.
Between two evils, I always picking the one I have never tried before.
e:
The error in the sentence lies in the verb tense: "picks" is incorrect. The adverb "always" indicates a habitual action, which requires the simple present tense. The subject "I" pairs with the base form of the verb "pick" in the simple present tense, not "picks" (which is used for third-person singular subjects).
Option 1 corrects the verb to "pick," making it grammatically correct: "I always pick."
Option 2 uses "is picking," which is present continuous and unsuitable for habitual actions.
Option 3 uses "picked," which is past tense and does not match the context of a general habit.
Option 4 uses "picking," which is a gerund/participle and grammatically incorrect here.
Thus, the correct option is 1: "Between two evils, I always pick the one I have never tried before."

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. She is the best dancer in the competition. She is a talented performer.
B. She is a best dancer in the competition. She is a talented performer.
C. She is the best dancer in competition. She is a talented performer.
D. She is the best dancer in competition. She is an talented performer.
e: A: Correct "The best dancer" is correct because "best" is a superlative adjective. A superlative adjective shall be followed by the definite article "the". And "a talented performer" is correct because "talented" starts with a consonant sound and aptly follows the indefinite article "a". This is because "a" is used before consonant-sounding words. B: Incorrect "A best dancer" is incorrect because "best" is a superlative, and superlatives should be used with "the." "A talented performer" is correct. C: Incorrect "The best dancer" is correct, but "in competition" should be "in the competition" to specify a particular competition. "A talented performer" is correct. D: Incorrect "In competition" should be "in the competition" to specify a particular competition. "An talented" is incorrect as "talented" starts with a consonant sound and requires the indefinite article "a" before it. This is because "an" is used before vowel-sounding words. Hence, option (d) is the answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun. · The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made. · The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared. · The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

t:
Identify the error in the following sentence and select the option with the correct use of the phrasal verb.
Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he blacked out.
o: Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he broke in.
Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he chickened out.
Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he checked out.
Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he turned down.
e:
The original sentence uses "blacked out," which means to lose consciousness or faint, but the context suggests Prateek simply lacked courage, not that he fainted. We need a phrasal verb that means avoiding or withdrawing due to fear or lack of courage.
· "Broke in" (Option 1) means to interrupt or enter forcibly, which doesn't fit.
· "Chickened out" (Option 2) means to withdraw from something due to fear or cowardice, which perfectly fits the context of failing to muster courage.
· "Checked out" (Option 3) means to leave or disengage, but it doesn't imply fear or cowardice.
· "Turned down" (Option 4) means to reject, which doesn't align with the situation.
Thus, Option 2 corrects the error appropriately: "Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he chickened out."

t:
Spot the erroneous part if any, in the following sentence.
Unless she/ <u>does not study(A)/</u> diligently, / <u>she won't(B)/</u> be able to/ <u>excel in(C)/</u> her exams. / No error (D).
e:
The adverbs 'until', 'unless', 'scarcely' and 'hardly' are already negative in tone and should not be followed by an additional 'not'. So, 'does not' needs to be removed and the verb form of 'study' be written accordingly in order to rectify the error. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.
The final correct sentence would be: Unless she studies diligently, she won't be able to excel in her exams.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: to witness the sunrise over the Himalayas.
e: Correction: Replace “the Northern India” with “Northern India”.The Basic Rule: We use the definite article 'the' before directions when they stand alone or refer to a specific point (e.g., The East, The South-West).The Exception (The Trap): We do not use an article before a direction if it is followed by the name of a place (e.g., North India, South Africa, West Bengal).Adjectives: Similarly, if a direction is used as an adjective like Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western before a proper noun, no article is used.Corrected Sentence - "The explorers travelled through Northern India before heading towards the East to witness the sunrise over the Himalayas."More Examples for Clarity-1. He is from South Africa. (No article)2. The sun rises in the East. ('The' is mandatory) 3. He lives in Western Europe. (No article)Things to Remember / Exam TipsThe "Of" Trigger: If you say "The North of India," the article returns because the "of" phrase makes it specific.The Place Name Rule: If a country/state name follows the direction (East Bengal, North Korea), drop the article.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error. 
He said me that he had finally decided to pursue his lifelong dream of travelling the world and writing about his adventures.
o: He said me that he had finally
decided to pursue his lifelong dream
e: In segment (a), "He said me" is incorrect. The correct phrase should be "He told me" where "told" is followed by the indirect object pronoun "me," indicating to whom the statement was addressed. "Told" is more appropriate here than "said" when reporting what someone said directly to another person. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. Note: An object pronoun is a type of pronoun used as the object of a verb or a preposition in a sentence. Object pronouns receive the action of the verb and are positioned after the verb or preposition. The corrected sentence: He told me that he had finally decided to pursue his lifelong dream of travelling the world and writing about his adventures.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: After the grueling interrogation, the suspect
was finally sent to the prison for a term
of ten years for his involvement in the heist.
e: Replace “the prison” with “prison”.Rule / Concept: Primary vs. Secondary Purpose - 'The' is not used before school, college, church, bed, table, hospital, market, or prison when these places are visited for their primary purpose (e.g., a criminal going to prison to serve a sentence).Since the suspect is going to prison as a prisoner (primary purpose), 'the' should not be used.More Examples for Clarity – I go to school every day. (To study) The injured man was taken to hospital. (For treatment)He goes to church on Sundays. (To pray)Things to Remember / Exam Tips - Use 'the' only if you are going to these places for a secondary purpose (e.g., "I went to the prison to meet the jailer").

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The team worked / diligent to finish / the project before / the deadline.
e: The segment with a grammatical error is 'diligent to finish'. "Diligent" (constant in effort to accomplish something) is an adjective, which is used to describe nouns. "Diligent" does not describe the verb "worked" properly. We need an adverb to modify the verb "worked". The adverb form of "diligent" is "diligently." Hence, (b) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: The team worked diligently to finish the project before the deadline.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
I am going / to buy a red car / with a leather seats / and a sunroof.
e: The article "a" is singular, but "seats" is plural. The correct form would be "with leather seats" (no article, as "leather" describes the material of the plural "seats") or "with a leather seat" (singular). The mismatch between "a" and "seats" is the error.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Although the deadline is approaching rapidly,
the construction crew completed only three-fourths
of the structural framework of the skyscraper so far.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “completed” with “has completed”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Present Perfect with "So Far" - The adverbial phrase "so far" (along with yet, already, up to now, till now) indicates a time period that began in the past and continues up to the present moment. this "bridge" between past and present requires the Present Perfect Tense (has/have + V3). Using the Simple Past (V2) with "so far" is a common error because it incorrectly treats a continuing situation as a finished, isolated event in the past. Use present perfect tense with these adverbs:- Yet, So far, Already, Just, just now, lately, recently, of late etc.💢 Application to the Given Question - The sentence mentions that the action of completing the structural framework is related to the present moment (indicated by "so far"). Therefore, the Simple Past "completed" is contextually incorrect. Since "the construction crew" is a collective noun acting as a single unit here, it should be paired with the singular present perfect form.

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The speaker's emphasiss is on the present-day problems that are being faced by ordinary men of India.
e:
The word 'emohasiss' is the incorrect spelling. 
The correct word is 'emphasis'. It means 'special importance, value, or prominence given to something'. Hence, option (a) is the answer.

t:
The following sentence has been split into three segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If the sentence is error free, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Arun did not join (1)/ the party because he has (2)/ an urgent work to do. (3)/ No error (4)
e: The correct sentence is "Arun did not join the party because he has some urgent work to do". Work when used in the context of matter or business is considered uncountable plural and therefore it should not be preceded by 'a' or 'an' whereas when referring to a creation or composition (poem, song, etc.) is countable and can be preceded by 'a' or 'an'. Urgent work, homework, class work, office work, important work etc. are uncountable and considered plural. C is the answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The chairperson of the high-level committee insisted that every member of the advisory board
be present at the upcoming annual general meeting to discuss the fiscal deficit
and that no one is allowed to leave the premises until a consensus is reached.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C). Replace “is” with “be”. 📌 Rule / Concept: The Mandative Present Subjunctive Mood Certain verbs (insist, suggest, demand, recommend, mandate) or adjectives (essential, vital, important) followed by the conjunction that require the base form of the verb (the subjunctive mood) in the following clause. This base form remains constant regardless of the tense of the main verb or the number/person of the subject. 💢 Application to the Given Question - The main verb of the sentence is insisted. This insistence governs two parallel clauses: "...that every member... be present" (Correctly used subjunctive). "...that no one is allowed..." (Incorrectly used indicative). Because the chairperson is still "insisting" on this second condition, the verb must also be in the base form (be) rather than the indicative form (is). More Examples for Clarity - Example 1 ✅ - The judge ordered that the defendant remain in custody. Example 2 ✅ - It is essential that he arrive on time for the hearing. Example 3 ✅- I suggest that she not be told about the surprise yet.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: While the initial costs of the infrastructure project were expected to be minimal, the additional expenses
resulting from the unforeseen environmental delays have been born entirely by the taxpayers,
leading to widespread public outcry and demands for a thorough government audit.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B).Replace “born” with “borne”.📌 Rule / Concept: Born vs. Borne Both words are past participles of the verb bear, but they are used in distinct contexts: Born: Used exclusively in the context of birth (e.g., "He was born in 1990"). In the passive voice, it is used only when not followed by the word "by".Borne: This is the versatile past participle used for all other meanings of bear—such as to carry, to support, to endure, or to produce. It is also used in the passive voice when followed by "by," even in the context of birth (though rare in modern exams).VERB FORM: Bear bore borne/born💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the context is about "carrying" or "sustaining" a financial burden (expenses). Since the meaning pertains to carrying/enduring a load rather than physical childbirth, the correct form is borne.More Examples for Clarity -Example 1: The grief was borne with great dignity by the widow. ✅Example 2: A new era of technology was born out of the industrial revolution. ✅Example 3: All the costs related to the shipping have been borne by the sender. ✅

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option.
These tips and tricks (A)/ once mastered, (B)/ will help you reach your search results (C)/ more faster than anyone else. (D)
e:
Part D has an error. 
The double comparative 'more faster' is grammatically incorrect. The correct usage is 'faster'. 
Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: These tips and tricks once mastered, will help you reach your search results faster than anyone else.

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
If the city's administration <u>had taken</u> stricter measures earlier, the waterlogging situation <u>will not have become</u> <u>so severe</u> <u>after the heavy rainfall</u>.
e: The error is in the main clause of this Type 3 conditional sentence in the segment will not have become. Type 3 conditionals are used to talk about unreal past situations. The structure is: If + Past Perfect, ... would/could/might + have + Past Participle (V3). The 'if' clause (If the city's administration had taken...) correctly uses the Past Perfect tense. Therefore, the main clause must use "would have + V3", not "will have + V3". Correct sentence: If the city's administration had taken stricter measures earlier, the waterlogging situation would not have become so severe after the heavy rainfall. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option.
Though we add few sugar / to our energy drinks / and fruit juices, they do have an excessive/ amount of calories.
o: and fruit juices, they do have an excessive
e:
In the given sentence, 'sugar' is an uncountable noun. We cannot use 'few/many' with uncountable nouns. With uncountable nouns, we use 'little/much'. So, 'few' should be replaced with 'little' to rectify the given sentence. Therefore, the error is in the part in option (b). Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.
The correct sentence is: Though we add little sugar to our energy drinks and fruit juices, they do have an excessive amount of calories.

t:
The following sentence has been split into three segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If the sentence is error free, mark 'No error' as your answer.
No sooner had she crossed a small bridge near the farm when/ the storm resumed/ with even greater intensity.
o: No sooner had she crossed a small bridge near the farm when
e:
Some adverbs are used in pairs- 'Hardly..when', 'no sooner.. than', 'scarcely..when', 'so..that', etc. So, the use of 'when' is inappropriate here. 'No sooner' is used to show that one thing happens immediately after another thing, so its usage seems appropriate here. It should be replaced with 'than'.
Alternatively, 'no sooner' can be replaced with 'hardly/scarcely'.
Hence, option (a) is correct.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Preeta wished she had not went to that party; it turned out to be quite boring.
e: The segment that contains a grammatical error is 'had not went'. The error is related to the verb "went." The use of the helping verb "had" in the sentence indicates the past perfect tense. When constructing a sentence with the past perfect tense, the main verb is typically in the past participle form, not the simple past form. However, the verb "went" is in the simple past form, not the past participle form. Therefore, "went" should be replaced with its past participle form "gone" to maintain grammatical correctness in the past perfect tense construction. Hence, (c) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: Preeta wished she had not gone to that party; it turned out to be quite boring. NOTE: "Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective."

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error.
The wedding gown / looked decently / despite being / studded with jewels.
e: When verbs of perception including look, taste, smell, feel and sound are used to express sensation or appearance, they are followed by adjectives, not adverbs. This means that 'looked' should be followed by 'decent' and not 'decently'. The correct sentence is: The wedding gown looked decent despite being studded with jewels. So, the part in option (c) has an error. Hence, option (c) is the answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: In the far corner of the dusty, abandoned library
was several rare manuscripts containing the lost
botanical records of the Victorian-era exploratory expeditions.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “was” with “were”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Full Inversion with Adverbials of Place When a sentence begins with a Prepositional Phrase of Place (In the corner, On the table, Under the bridge), and the main verb is a verb of state, position, or existence (be, stand, sit, lie, exist), the sentence undergoes Full Inversion. In this structure, the entire verb or verb phrase comes before the subject. The most common error in competitive exams is "Subject-Verb Agreement." The verb must agree with the subject that follows it, not the noun inside the prepositional phrase. 💢 Application to the Given Question In the far corner of the dusty, abandoned library was several rare manuscripts... In this sentence, the phrase "In the far corner of the dusty, abandoned library" is the adverbial of place. The real subject of the sentence is "several rare manuscripts," which is plural. Therefore, using the singular auxiliary verb "was" is grammatically incorrect. It must be changed to the plural form "were" to match the subject Corrected Sentence In the far corner of the dusty, abandoned library were several rare manuscripts containing the lost botanical records of the Victorian-era exploratory expeditions.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error.
It is bestest to use your calories wisely by filling them up with micronutrient-filled foods.
e:
The segment mentioned in option (c) has an error. In formal English language, no such word like 'bestest' exists. The correct word to be used is 'best' which is the superlative form of adjective 'good'.
Hence, option (c) is correct.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: circulating unverified reports on social media.
e: The correct answer is - option A. Replace “not only restrained publishing” with “restrained not only publishing”.Rule/Concept: Conjunction & Parallelism –Parallelism refers to the grammatical principle that the elements joined by correlative conjunctions must be identical in structure and form. In the construction “not only … but also”, both parts must belong to the same grammatical category and follow the same syntactic pattern to maintain balance and clarity. If a noun is used after not only, a noun must follow but also. If a verb phrase is used after not only, a verb phrase must follow but also. If an adjective, adverb, infinitive, or prepositional phrase is used after not only, the same form must follow but also. Correct: She is not only honest but also diligent. (adjective + adjective) Incorrect: She is not only honest but also works hard. (adjective + verb phrase → lack of parallelism)Corrected Sentence - The court restrained not only publishing sensitive information but also circulating unverified reports on social media.

t: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
o: All of the essential equipment for the camping trip, including the tents and sleeping bags, have been carefully packed in the back of the car.
All of the essential equipment for the camping trip, including the tents and sleeping bags, are carefully packed in the back of the car.
All of the essential equipments for the camping trip, including the tents and sleeping bags, have been carefully packed in the back of the car.
All of the essential equipment for the camping trip, including the tents and sleeping bags, has been carefully packed in the back of the car.
e: This question tests subject-verb agreement with uncountable nouns. The word "equipment" is an uncountable noun, which means it does not have a plural form and is always treated as singular. · Subject: "All of the essential equipment" (The true subject is "equipment," which is singular). · Verb: Must be singular ("has been packed"). Let's analyze the options: · a) This sentence incorrectly uses the plural verb "have been." The verb must agree with the singular noun "equipment," not the plural nouns in the interrupting phrase ("tents and sleeping bags"). · b) This sentence uses the plural verb "are," which is also incorrect. · c) This sentence incorrectly pluralizes the uncountable noun "equipment" to "equipments" and uses a plural verb. · d) This sentence is grammatically correct. It correctly treats "equipment" as a singular noun and uses the singular verb "has been." The correct sentence is: All of the essential equipment for the camping trip, including the tents and sleeping bags, has been carefully packed in the back of the car. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. 
Overtaking those cyclists on an Alpine climb are a dozen times harder than on the flat.
e: The subject of the given sentence is the gerund 'overtaking' which is singular in nature. According to subject-verb agreement, a singular verb should be used with a singular subject. So, the plural verb 'are' should be replaced with its singular form 'is' to rectify the given sentence. The error is in the segment in option (b). Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: Overtaking those cyclists on an Alpine climb is a dozen times harder than on the flat. Note: Gerund: Gerund is a verb form that functions as a noun, ending in -ing. A gerund can be either the subject or object of a sentence in English. Example: "Everybody enjoyed her dancing and singing at the party." The words 'dancing' and 'singing' are gerunds. Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The antique clock, which has been <u>in our family</u> <u>for generations, need</u> <u>urgent repairs by</u> <u>a skilled horologist</u>.
e: The error is in the segment "for generations, need". The subject of the main clause is "The antique clock". The phrase "which has been in our family for generations" is a relative clause describing the clock. "Clock" is a singular noun. Therefore, it requires a singular verb. The verb "need" is in its plural form (or base form used with plural subjects and I/you). The singular form for a third-person singular subject in the present tense is "needs". Correct sentence: The antique clock, which has been in our family for generations, needs urgent repairs by a skilled horologist. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: · Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb] · A restrictive relative clause (also known as a defining relative clause) gives essential information about a noun that comes before it: without this clause the sentence wouldn't make much sense. A restrictive relative clause can be introduced by that, which, whose, who, or whom. Comma is not used before a restrictive clause. A non-restrictive relative clause (also called a non-defining relative clause) provides extra information that could be left out without affecting the meaning or structure of the sentence. Non-restrictive relative clauses are normally introduced by which, whose, who, or whom, but never by that. Comma is used before a non-restrictive clause.

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “before”: The audience had already left the auditorium before the organizers could announce the results of the competition.
e: Answer: B) Conjunction Explanation: A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases, or clauses. When a word connects two clauses, it functions as a conjunction. Here, “before” connects these two clauses: The audience had already left the auditorium the organizers could announce the results Since it joins two clauses together, “before” is a subordinating conjunction.

t:
In the following question, a sentence is given, divided into three parts, which may or may not contain an error. Mark the option containing the part with the error. If the sentence is error free, mark 'No error' as the answer. 
Raju has(A)/ passed the matriculation (B)/ examination in 1999(C).
e:
Part A has an error. The given sentence talks of a specific time, i.e., 1999 in the past. So, the use of the Present Perfect tense 'has passed' is incorrect and hence it should be made Simple Past tense [passed] by removing 'has' from the sentence, which rectifies the error. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. 
The final sentence would be: Raju passed the matriculation examination in 1999.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

Along the northern border of India is seen the Himalayas tall, mighty and majestic in their unique splendour.
o: Along the northern border of India
e:
'The Himalayas' is a plural noun (refers to a series of ranges), so a plural verb 'are' would be appropriate in place of singular verb 'is'.
Along the northern border of India are seen the Himalayas tall, mighty and majestic in their unique splendour.
Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

t: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
o: A house like this needs a particular kind of configuration and furnishing.
The artist completed the masterpiece of using a unique blend of colours and textures.
The airport was bustling with activity as many aircrafts prepared for departure.
The committee planned to reviewed the proposal during their next meeting.
e: The sentence given in option (a) is grammatically correct. Option (b) is incorrect. The error lies in the incorrect use of the preposition "of" instead of "by." When we want to indicate the method or means by which something is done, we use the preposition "by." The preposition "of" is used to indicate possession, origin, or association, but it does not correctly convey the idea of the method or means by which the masterpiece was completed. The correct sentence is: The artist completed the masterpiece by using a unique blend of colours and textures. Option (c) is also incorrect. The word "aircrafts" is incorrect. The correct plural form is "aircraft" (singular and plural are the same). The correct sentence is: The airport was bustling with activity as many aircraft prepared for departure. Option (d) is also incorrect. After the infinitive marker "to", we usually use the base form of the verb. But 'reviewed' (past tense form) is not the base form. So, 'reviewed' should be replaced with the base form 'review'. The correct sentence is: The committee planned to review the proposal during their next meeting. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. NOTE: A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples I. The teacher scolded the child for being late. II. We're going to a party. · The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition. · The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object. "Infinitive: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, often preceded by to. Consider the sentences given below: · To err is human. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to err' is the subject of the verb 'is'] · My father likes to cook. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to cook' is the object of the verb 'likes'] · To vote in elections is our right. [the infinitive 'to vote', like a noun, is the subject of the verb 'is', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (elections)] · Radha went to the lake to fetch water. [the infinitive 'to fetch', like a noun, is the object of the verb 'went', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (water)] · The above sentences illustrate various ways in which infinitives are used. It can both act as a noun and a verb."

t:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
Police could not catch / the gunman as he ran off / so very fastly into the woods.
o: the gunman as he ran off
so very fastly into the woods.
e:
The correct adverb form of 'fast' is 'fast' only. 'Fastly' should be replaced with 'fast'. 
The correct sentence is: Police could not catch the gunman as he ran off so very fast into the woods.
Hence, option (d) is the answer.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
He didn't / called me / in the / last week.
e:
'Didn't' takes the base verb ('call', in this case) after it, so the usage of 'called' (past simple (V2)/ past participle (V3)) is incorrect.
Hence, (c) is the correct answer.

t:
In the following question, a sentence is given, divided into three parts, which may or may not contain an error. Mark the option containing the part with the error. If the sentence is error free, mark 'No error' as the answer. 
Aeon has (A)/ not do his homework (B)/ from school yet(C).
e:
Part B has an error. The verb used after 'has' should always be in the past participle form. So, the present tense verb 'do' is to be replaced by the past participle verb 'done' in order to rectify the error. Hence, (d) is the correct answer. 
Past participle is the form of a verb, typically ending in -ed in English, which is used in forming perfect and passive tenses. 
The final sentence would be: Aeon has not done his homework from school yet.
