t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: During the annual general meeting, the Board
of Directors’s decision regarding the bonus structure
was met with a standing ovation from the shareholders.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace Directors’s with Directors’.Rule/Concept: Possession in Compound Nouns & Plural Nouns -When a noun is a Compound Noun or a Collective Title (like Board of Directors), and we need to show possession, the apostrophe is placed at the end of the entire phrase.However, there is a specific sub-rule for plural nouns ending in -s:-If the word/phrase ends in a plural -s, we only add an apostrophe ( ' ) without an additional s.-For "Board of Directors," the primary noun "Directors" is already plural and ends in s. Therefore, to show possession, we only add the apostrophe after the s.In this sentence, "Board of Directors" is treated as a single entity or a plural body. Since the final word "Directors" is a plural noun ending in s, adding another 's creates an awkward and incorrect "s-s" sound. The correct possessive form for a plural ending in s is simply the apostrophe at the end.Corrected Sentence - During the annual general meeting, the Board of Directors’ decision regarding the bonus structure was met with a standing ovation from the shareholders.Things to Remember/Exam Tips - -Pluralization vs. Possession: To pluralize a compound noun, add 's' to the root word (Commanders-in-chief). To show possession, add the apostrophe to the last word (Commander-in-chief's).-The S-Rule: If the last word of the group is a plural ending in s, just add the apostrophe ('). If it doesn't end in s, add 's.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The spiritual leaders emphasized that the
practice of meditation has been an integral
part of our civilization for time immemorial.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C). Replace “for” with “since” (or “from”). 📌 Rule / Concept: USE OF SINCE/FOR - Since (point of time):- 7 am, 2007, winter, childhood, last week / month / year/decade, time immemorial etc. For(duration of time):- 7 minutes, a long time, a while, 2 hours/weeks/months/years, the last 2 days/weeks/months/years etc. 💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the usage of "for" is the error. Because the sentence uses the Present Perfect tense ("has been"), it is describing a state that started at a point in the distant past and continues today. Therefore, the "point of time" preposition "since" (highly preferred by SSC) or the idiomatic "from" must be used instead of the "period of time" preposition "for."

t: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
o: The ebb and flow of the stock market prices, which is influenced by global economic policies and investor sentiment, often serves as a barometer for the nation's financial health.
The ebb and flow of the stock market prices, which are influenced by global economic policies and investor sentiment, often serves as a barometer for the nation's financial health.
The ebb and flow of the stock market prices, which are influenced by global economic policies and investor sentiment, often serve as a barometer for the nation's financial health.
The ebb and flow of the stock market prices, which is influenced by global economic policies and investor sentiment, often serve as a barometer for the nation's financial health.
e: This question involves two different subject-verb agreement rules: a compound subject that forms a single idea, and a verb in a relative clause. · Main Subject: "The ebb and flow" (a single, unified concept, hence singular). · Main Verb: Must be singular ("serves"). · Relative Clause: "which are influenced..." The antecedent of "which" is "prices" (plural), so the verb in the clause must be plural ("are"). Let's analyze the options: · a) The main verb "serves" is correct, but the verb in the relative clause "is" is incorrect. It should be "are" to agree with its antecedent "prices." · b) This sentence is perfectly correct. The main verb "serves" (singular) agrees with the singular concept "The ebb and flow." The verb in the relative clause "are" (plural) correctly agrees with its antecedent "prices." · c) The verb in the relative clause "are" is correct, but the main verb "serve" (plural) is incorrect. It does not agree with the singular subject "The ebb and flow." · d) Both verbs in this sentence are incorrect. "is" in the relative clause should be "are," and "serve" in the main clause should be "serves." The correct sentence is: The ebb and flow of the stock market prices, which are influenced by global economic policies and investor sentiment, often serves as a barometer for the nation's financial health. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The investigative journalist finally managed to track down the
whistleblower who the intelligence agencies had been searching for
since the classified documents were leaked to the public.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “who” with “whom”.📌 Rule / Concept: Who vs. Whom (Subjective vs. Objective Case)-Who: This is the subjective case. It is used when the pronoun is the doer of the action (the subject of the verb).-Whom: This is the objective case. It is used when the pronoun is the receiver of the action (the object of the verb or preposition).Application to the Given Question"...the whistleblower who the intelligence agencies had been searching for..."In this clause, we have a clear subject: "the intelligence agencies." The action is: "had been searching for." The whistleblower is not the one doing the searching; he is the object being searched for. Since the relative pronoun refers to the object of the verb "searching for," we must use the objective case "whom."

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The environmentalists expressed grave concern that Nile,
which has been the lifeblood of Egypt for millennia, is facing
unprecedented levels of pollution due to rapid industrialization.
e: Replace “Nile” with “the Nile”.Rule / Concept: Use of 'The' with Geographical Entities – The definite article 'the' must be used before the names of specific geographical features such as oceans (The Pacific), seas (The Red Sea), rivers (The Amazon), deserts (The Gobi), and mountain ranges (The Alps). These are unique, large-scale natural entities, and 'the' is used to provide the necessary definiteness to their proper names.Corrected Sentence- The environmentalists expressed grave concern that the Nile, which has been the lifeblood of Egypt for millennia, is facing unprecedented levels of pollution due to rapid industrialization.Things to Remember / Exam Tips-Ranges vs. Peaks: This is the biggest trap. Use 'the' for ranges (The Himalayas, The Rockies) but NEVER use 'the' for individual peaks (Mount Everest, K2, Annapurna).The "Specific" River: Even if the word "River" isn't written (e.g., "The Nile" instead of "The Nile River"), the article 'the' remains mandatory.

t:
The following sentence has an error in its tense. Identify the error and select the correct sentence from the options.
If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allow you to go.
o: If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.
If you apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.
If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would allow you to go.
If you can apprise me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.
e: This is a conditional sentence expressing an unreal past condition (third conditional). The error is in the main clause where "allow" should be in past participle form as "allowed" since it follows the modal auxiliary "would have." The correct structure for third conditional sentences is: "If + past perfect, would/could/might + have + past participle." 1 correctly uses "had apprised" in the if-clause and "would have allowed" in the main clause.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: For the last three decades, the
to eradicate illiteracy in rural belts.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “worked” with “has worked”. Rule / Concept: Present Perfect vs. Simple Past (Duration vs. Point of Time) The Present Perfect Tense (has/have + V3) is used to describe an action that started in the past and continues up to the present moment, or has relevance to the present. It is frequently used with time markers like "For" (duration) or "Since" (starting point). In contrast, the Simple Past (V2) is used for actions that were completed at a specific point in the past and have no direct continuity with the present. 💢 Application to the Given Question For the last three decades, the non-profit organization worked tirelessly to eradicate illiteracy in rural belts. The sentence begins with the time phrase "For the last three decades," which implies a duration of time that stretches from thirty years ago right up to the current moment. Using the Simple Past "worked" suggests the organization no longer exists or has stopped its work. To show that the work is an ongoing commitment or a state that characterizes the organization today, the Present Perfect "has worked" (or Present Perfect Continuous "has been working") must be used. Corrected Sentence For the last three decades, the non-profit organization has worked tirelessly to eradicate illiteracy in rural belts.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The watchman(A)/ of our (B) / building(C)/ has a car also(D).
e:
Part D has an error. The conjunction 'also' is usually used in the middle or beginning of a sentence and not at the end. Hence, (d) is the correct answer. 
The final sentence would be: The watchman of our building also has a car.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Whenever the eccentric professor begins his
lecture with a series of unintentional puns,
we cannot help but to laugh at him.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “to laugh” with “laugh”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Bare Infinitives after "Cannot help but" the structure "Cannot help but" is a fixed idiomatic expression. The "but" in this phrase functions similarly to "except." When this specific combination is used, it must be followed by a Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to"). It is crucial to distinguish this from the phrase "Cannot help" (without the "but"), which requires a Gerund (V{ing}). Structure 1: Cannot help + V{ing} (e.g., I cannot help laughing.) Structure 2: Cannot help but + V1 (e.g., I cannot help but laugh.) 💢 Application to the Given Question "...we cannot help but to laugh at him." In this sentence, the phrase "cannot help but" is used. Following the rules of this idiomatic construction, the verb that follows must be in its base form (V1). The inclusion of "to" before "laugh" creates a full infinitive, which is grammatically incorrect in this specific context. Corrected Sentence Whenever the eccentric professor begins his lecture with a series of unintentional puns, we cannot help but laugh at him.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The judicial committee noted that the evidence presented by
the defense was too much circumstantial to warrant an
immediate acquittal of the accused in the high-profile case.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) 👉 Replace “too much” with “much too”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Much too vs. Too much Too much is used as an Adjective before Nouns (specifically uncountable nouns). Much too is used as an Adverb before Adjectives. simple way to remember this is the "Last Word Rule": Too much + Noun (e.g., too much work) Much too + Adjective (e.g., much too heavy) 💢 Application to the Given Question ...the defense was too much circumstantial to warrant... In this sentence, the word circumstantial is an Adjective (describing the nature of the evidence). According to the rule, we cannot use "too much" to modify an adjective; we must use much too. Therefore, "too much circumstantial" is grammatically incorrect and must be replaced with "much too circumstantial." Corrected Sentence The judicial committee noted that the evidence presented by the defense was much too circumstantial to warrant an immediate acquittal of the accused in the high-profile case. More Examples for Clarity Example 1 This task is much too difficult for a beginner to handle alone. (Adjective) ✅ Example 2 There is too much salt in the soup. (Noun) ✅ Incorrect Usage Wrong example 1 This room is too much small for all of us. (Small is an adjective) ❌ Wrong example 2 I have much too work to finish by tonight. (Work is a noun) ❌ 🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips The Adjective Test: If you can put "very" before the word (e.g., very circumstantial, very hot, very tall), it is an adjective, and you must use much too. The Noun Test: If the word represents a thing or quantity (e.g., sugar, noise, patience), use too much

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Having been reached the final destination
after a grueling ten-hour journey, the weary
travelers checked into the nearest hotel.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “Having been reached” with “Having reached”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Active Perfect Participle (Having + V3) The Perfect Participle expresses an action completed before the main action of the sentence. Active Voice (Having + V3): Used when the subject performs the action. Passive Voice (Having + been + V3): Used when the subject receives the action. 💢 Application to the Given Question "Having been reached the final destination..." In this sentence, the "weary travelers" (the subject) are the ones who performed the act of reaching the destination. They were not "reached" by someone else. Using the passive form "Having been reached" is logically incorrect here. We must use the active form "Having reached" to show that the travelers completed their journey before checking into the hotel. Corrected Sentence Having reached the final destination after a grueling ten-hour journey, the weary travelers checked into the nearest hotel.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The brilliance of Sir Isaac Newton lies in
the fact that he invented the law of universal
gravitation after observing an apple fall.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B).👉 Replace “invented” with “discovered”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Confusing Pairs of Verbs (Discover vs. Invent) -Discover (V1) – Discovered (V2/V3): To find or become aware of something that already existed in nature but was unknown to others (e.g., gravity, planets, chemical elements, hidden islands).Invent (V1) – Invented (V2/V_3): To create, design, or produce something that did not exist before through original thought or experiment (e.g., the steam engine, the internet, a new recipe).Application to the Given Question - Gravity is a natural force that has existed since the beginning of the universe; Newton did not "create" it in a lab or design it from scratch. He observed it, formulated the mathematical laws for it, and made it known to the world. Therefore, the correct verb is discovered. Using "invented" would implies Newton manufactured gravity himself, which is logically incorrect.More Examples for Clarity - Example 1: Columbus discovered America, but he did not invent it. (Land already existed).Example 2: Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin in 1793. (A new machine) Example 3: Scientists have discovered a new species of frog in Western Ghats. (Species already existed)

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The variety of colourful tropical bird species
inhabiting the deep lush green Amazon rainforest
are attracting many eager tourists every year.
e: The Correct Ans is - Option (C)The plural verb "are" must be replaced with the singular verb "is."Rule/Concept: "The variety of" Agreement In competitive exams, the choice between "A" and "The" completely changes the verb:The variety of... = Singular Verb. (It focuses on the single group or the concept of variety itself).A variety of... = Plural Verb. (It acts as a synonym for "many" or "various").Correct Sentence: The variety of colourful tropical bird species inhabiting the deep lush green Amazon rainforest is attracting many eager tourists every year.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
The weather was so bad / during the storm as we could not / venture out of our / house for two days.
o: during the storm as we could not
e: The error lies in the conjunction pair used to show cause and effect. The adverb 'so' is followed by the conjunction 'that' to express a result or consequence. The pair is 'so..that..'. Using 'as' is incorrect in this structure. Correct sentence: The weather was so bad during the storm that we could not venture out of our house for two days. So, there is an error in the part mentioned in option b). Hence, option (b) is the answer. Note: A conjunction (also called a connective) is a word such as and, because, but, for, if, or, when etc. Conjunctions are used to connect phrases, clauses, and sentences.

t:
Spot the erroneous part if any, in the following sentence. 
<u>Having being in the company(A)/</u> for over a decade, / <u>Michael was well-versed in(B)/</u> the intricacies of the industry/ <u>and had developed strong(C)</u>/ relationships with clients. / No error (D).
e: "Having" is a gerund or present participle form of the verb "have," which is used to indicate an ongoing action or state. However, in this context, we need the past participle form of the verb. "Being" is the present participle, which is used in continuous tenses (e.g., "is being," "was being"), and it's inappropriate here because the sentence refers to a past and completed action. "Having been" is the correct past perfect participle form, used to indicate a completed action in the past that is relevant to the present or another past event. In this sentence, it implies that Michael's long presence in the company led to his expertise and relationships. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. The correct sentence: Having been in the company for over a decade, Michael was well-versed in the intricacies of the industry and had developed strong relationships with clients. Note: Gerund: Gerund is a verb form that functions as a noun, ending in -ing. A gerund can be either the subject or object of a sentence in English. Example: "Everybody enjoyed her dancing and singing at the party." The words 'dancing' and 'singing' are gerunds. Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.
Either of the candidates have conveyed to the / leadership that they will only / reveal their names next week.
o: Either of the candidates have conveyed to the
e:
The phrase 'either of' is always followed by a plural noun and a singular verb. So, the plural verb 'have' should be replaced with its singular verb 'has' to rectify the given sentence.
Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.
The correct sentence is: Either of the candidates has conveyed to the leadership that they would only reveal their names next week.

t:
Select the option that contains a grammatical error in the underlined portion.
Yesterday, I went to the ballet class with my elder sister and, we will shoot a video for our YouTube channel.
o: <u>Yesterday, I went to the ballet</u> class with my elder sister and, we will shoot a video for our YouTube channel.
Yesterday, I went to the ballet <u>class with my elder sister</u> and, we will shoot a video for our YouTube channel.
Yesterday, I went to the ballet class with my elder sister <u>and, we will shoot</u> a video for our YouTube channel.
Yesterday, I went to the ballet class with my elder sister and, we will shoot <u>a video for our YouTube channel. </u>
e: The whole sentence is in past tense [evident from 'yesterday'], so 'will shoot' [future tense] should be replaced with 'shot' [past tense] to rectify the error. The correct sentence is: Yesterday, I went to the ballet class with my elder sister and, we shot a video for our YouTube channel. Hence, (c) is the correct answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: During the peak of the winter season, the
mechanical gears of the clock tower got
freeze due to the lack of proper lubrication.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C). Replace “freeze” with “frozen”.📌 Rule/Concept: The Passive "Get" and Past Participles – When we use the verb "get" (or become/be) to describe a change in state or a passive action, it must be followed by the Past Participle (V3) form of the verb, not the base form (V1). The past participle acts as an adjective describing the subject's condition.V1 (Base): Freeze V2 (Past): Froze V3 (Past Participle): Frozen 💢 Application to the Given Question- In this sentence, "got" indicates a transition into a new state. The gears did not perform the action of freezing; they became in a state of being frozen. Therefore, the base form "freeze" is grammatically incorrect. To describe the state of the gears, we must use the V3 form: frozen.Incorrect: The water got freeze.Correct: The water got frozen. (or "The water froze.")Things to Remember / Exam TipsThe "Done" Rule: Whenever you see Get/Got, Become/Became, or Is/Are/Was/Were, ask yourself if the subject is doing the action or experiencing a state. If it's a state, use V3.Common "Got" Collocations: Got tired, got bored, got stuck, got broken, got frozen.Verb vs. Adjective: Remember that while "froze" is a verb (The water froze), "frozen" is the form used after helping verbs to describe the result.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: from the wreckage of the ship
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C).Replace “were” with “was”.📌 Rule / Concept: Singular Indefinite Pronouns indefinite pronouns that end in -thing (Everything, Something, Nothing, Anything), -one, or -body are always singular. Even when these pronouns are followed by a relative clause (like "that was salvaged...") or a long prepositional phrase, the main verb of the sentence must agree with the singular subject.In this sentence, the subject is "Everything." The phrase "that was salvaged from the wreckage of the ship" is a relative clause providing more information about the subject, but it does not change the subject's grammatical number. Since "Everything" is singular, the main verb must also be singular. Therefore, "were" (plural) is incorrect and must be changed to "was" (singular).REMEMBER THE LIST: Everybody, everything, everyone, somebody, someone, something, nobody, no one, nothing, anybody, anyone, anything; use singular verbs with these pronouns.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Despite his immense interest in classical music,
the young prodigy usually has not practiced
his violin lessons for more than an hour daily.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “has not” with “does not”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Simple Present for Habitual Actions When a sentence describes a habit, routine, or frequency, we must use the Simple Present Tense . Adverbs of frequency such as usually, often, seldom, daily, always, and never act as "tense markers" that point toward the Simple Present. Using the Present Perfect is incorrect here because the Present Perfect is used for actions that happened at an unspecified time in the past or have just been completed. It does not denote a general habit. 💢 Application to the Given Question "...the young prodigy usually has not practiced his violin lessons for more than an hour daily." The sentence contains two major indicators of a habit: The word "usually" (denoting frequency). The word "daily" (denoting a routine). Because the sentence is describing the prodigy's regular routine (or lack thereof), we must use the negative form of the Simple Present. Since "the young prodigy" is a singular subject, we use "does not" followed by the base form of the verb (practice). Corrected Sentence Despite his immense interest in classical music, the young prodigy usually does not practice his violin lessons for more than an hour daily.

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error. 
<u>The</u> judge <u>adjourn</u> the court proceedings <u>until</u> further <u>notice</u>.
e: The part that contains the error is 'adjourn'. The error lies in the subject-verb agreement. The subject of the sentence is "judge," which is singular. But the verb "adjourn" is plural. The verb needs to be conjugated correctly for the singular subject. Therefore, to correct the error, the plural verb 'adjourn' should be replaced with the singular verb 'adjourns' to match the singular subject "judge". Hence, (d) is the correct answer. Or simply, replace 'adjourn' with its past form 'adjourned' to rectify the error. The correct sentence is: The judge adjourns the court proceedings until further notice. Or The judge adjourned the court proceedings until further notice. NOTE: Subject-verb agreement means that a subject and its verb must be both singular or plural: A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. For example, in the sentence 'John lives in France', the subject John (singular 'he') 'agrees with' the third person singular form of the verb to live - lives.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. 
Radhika wanted to / know my views of / the plan regarding the / Shimla trip next weekend.
e: The nouns like 'dependence, pity, views, attack, impression, etc.' are followed by the preposition 'on'. So, the preposition 'of' in the sentence makes it grammatically incorrect. Replace it with the preposition 'on' to rectify the error. Correct sentence: Radhika wanted to know my views on the plan regarding the Shimla trip next weekend. So, option c) is the segment that contains a grammatical error. Hence, option c) is correct. Note: A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples 1) The teacher scolded the child for being late. 2) We're going to a party. · The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition. · The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. The photo captured an beautiful sunset. It was captured during an our vacation in the Maldives.
B. A photo captured an beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in the Maldives.
C. An photo captured the beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in a Maldives.
D. The photo captured a beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in the Maldives.
e: The definite article 'the' should be used before 'photo' and 'Maldives' because in both instances, it introduces specific nouns, that is, 'a particular photo that captured a sunset' and 'a place (Maldives)'. The indefinite article 'a' should be used before 'beautiful' as it is referring to an unspecified noun, that is, 'sunset'. Since 'beautiful' is not a vowel-sounding word, 'an' cannot be used before it. The sentences A, B, and C depict grammatically incorrect usage of the articles. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Troy <u>is</u> the city <u>who</u> was <u>destroyed</u> in a day by the <u>intruders</u>.
e: We use the relative pronoun 'who' to refer to humans and we use 'that' to refer to inanimate objects, types of people, places, things, or animals. Since the city 'Troy' [a place] is mentioned in the sentence which is referred to using the relative pronoun, 'who' needs to be replaced by 'that' in order to rectify the error. The correct sentence is: Troy is the city that was destroyed in a day by the intruders. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. Note: Relative pronouns: A relative pronoun is used to connect a clause or phrase to a noun or pronoun. The clause modifies, or describes, the noun. The most common relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that. For example: She is the girl who received the award for bravery from our Home Minister.

t:
In the question given below, one part of the sentence may or may not have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. 
You need to(A)/ constantly target(B)/ your bicep by(C)/ using a curl rod(D).
e:
Part C has an error. Some nouns are used only in the plural forms. Some examples are: jeans, trousers, pants, tights, shorts, pyjamas, scissors, etc. 'Biceps' is one such word. So, 'bicep' needs to be replaced by 'biceps' in the given sentence in order to rectify the error. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

t:
The
following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the
segment that contains a grammatical error.
e:
The error is that "envious" should be replaced with "jealous", as "envious" typically implies a desire for something someone else has, whereas "jealous" implies a sense of insecurity or threat.


"Envious" typically implies a desire for something someone else has, often with a sense of resentment or bitterness. For example:


- She was envious of her friend's success.
- He was envious of his neighbour’s luxurious car.


"Jealous", on the other hand, typically implies a sense of insecurity or threat, often related to a personal relationship or possession. For example:


- She was jealous of the attention her partner was giving to someone else.
- He was jealous of his brother's influence over their parents.
To illustrate the difference:
- If someone has a nice car, you might be envious of their car.
- But if your partner is spending too much time with someone else, you might be jealous of the attention they're receiving.
In the context of the original sentence: Both words could work, but "jealous" might be a slightly better choice to convey the idea that Mrs Verma feels threatened or insecure about her relationship with her husband.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
In order to connect / these themes to a wider / historical context, Rahul go / beyond aesthetic analysis.
e: The error is in "Rahul go." The subject "Rahul" is third-person singular, requiring the verb "goes" (present tense, third-person singular), thereby introducing error in subject-verb agreement. The correct segment should be "historical context, Rahul goes." The correct sentence is: In order to connect these themes to a wider historical context, Rahul goes beyond aesthetic analysis. Hence, the correct answer is option (4). Note: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: During the high-profile investigation, the lead lobbyist
was accused of consistently seeking their favour in exchange
for awarding lucrative government contracts to his clients.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “their favour” with “favour of them” or “favour from them”.Rule/Concept: Nouns that Reject Possessive Adjectives – As we established with words like leave and separation, the word favour is grammatically restricted in formal English. You cannot "own" a favour using a possessive pronoun (my, your, his, her, their).✅ Corrected Sentence - During the high-profile investigation, the lead lobbyist was accused of consistently seeking favour of them in exchange for awarding lucrative government contracts to his clients.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The sociologists argued that the children who are
raised in multicultural environments tend to develop
a more inclusive worldview than those who are not.
e: Replace “the children” with “children”.Rule / Concept: Omission of Articles before Plural Nouns in a General Sense – When a plural noun is used to represent a whole class, category, or a general truth, it does not take the definite article 'the'. We only use 'the' with plural nouns when we are referring to a specific group of people or things that have already been mentioned or are identified by a following phrase.Corrected Sentence- The sociologists argued that children who are raised in multicultural environments tend to develop a more inclusive worldview than those who are not.More Examples for Clarity-1. Books are our best friends. (General sense)2. The books on that shelf are mine. (Specific sense)Things to Remember / Exam Tips-General vs. Specific: Always ask yourself: "Am I talking about all [nouns] in the world or a specific set?" If it's all, remove 'the'.Abstract Concepts: This rule also applies to uncountable nouns like Gold, Honesty, or Water when used generally.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.
Either Ramesh or Reema have the keys to the cupboard.
e: The segment that contains a grammatical error is 'or Reema have'. The error lies in subject-verb agreement. The subject "Either Ramesh or Reema" is a compound subject joined by the conjunction "or." When dealing with compound subjects joined by "or," the verb should agree with the subject closest to it. In the given case, the subject "Reema" (singular) is closer to the verb. However, the verb "have" is plural, which does not agree with the singular subject. Therefore, the correct verb form should be "has" to match the singular subject "Reema." Other segments of the sentence are grammatically correct. Hence, (d) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: Either Ramesh or Reema has the keys to the cupboard. NOTE: Subject-verb agreement means that a subject and its verb must be both singular or both plural: A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. For example, in the sentence 'John lives in France', the subject John (singular 'he') 'agrees with' the third person singular form of the verb to live - lives. "CONJUNCTIONS A conjunction (also called a connective) is a word such as and, because, but, for, if, or, when etc. Conjunctions are used to connect phrases, clauses, and sentences."

t:
In the following question, a sentence is given which is divided into four parts. Out of the four parts, one part contains an error. Mark that option as your answer. 
Not only the students but also (A)/ the coach have convinced the (B)/ management that they should only (C)/ reveal the name next week. (D)
e:
Part B has an error. 
When not only..but also combines two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. So, the auxiliary verb 'have' should be replaced with its singular form 'has' to justify the singular subject 'coach'. 
Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: Not only the students but also the coach has convinced the management that they should only reveal the name next week.

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “that”: The proposal that the senior researchers submitted after months of fieldwork was finally approved by the international review board.
e: Answer: A) Relative Pronoun Explanation: A relative pronoun is a pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers back to a noun mentioned earlier in the sentence. Common relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that. Here, “that” refers back to the noun “proposal” and introduces the clause: “that the senior researchers submitted after months of fieldwork”. This clause gives additional information about the proposal. Since “that” both refers to the noun and connects the clause, it is a relative pronoun.

t: Select the sentence that has a grammatical error.
e: The sentence with a grammatical error is 'Rama can bowl fastly.' The error lies in the word "fastly." The correct adverb form of "fast" is "fast", not 'fastly'. Other sentences are grammatically correct. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The grieving widow, supported by her relatives and local clergy,
fervently prayed that her only son, who had been missing for weeks,
is restored to life and returned to his family by some divine intervention.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) - Replace “is” with “be”. 📌 Rule / Concept: The Subjunctive Mood (Prayers and Wishes) The Present Subjunctive is used in "that-clauses" that express a prayer, a wish, or a hope for a state of being that is not yet a reality. In formal the verb following "prayed that" or "wished that" must be in its base form (be), not the indicative form (is, am, or are). 💢 Application to the Given Question - The verb prayed acts as the trigger for the subjunctive mood in the subordinate clause. Even though the subject "son" is singular, the indicative verb is is incorrect in this formal context of a prayer. It must be replaced with the base form be to correctly reflect the subjunctive mood. More Examples for Clarity Example 1 ✅ They prayed that the rain cease before the harvest. (Not ceases) Example 2 ✅ We pray that he be granted a swift recovery. (Not is) Example 3 ✅ I pray that God bless you. (Not blesses)

t:
Select the grammatically correct sentence. 
A) Rohini have been working on this project for two weeks. She needs to complete the final report in the next 10 days.
B) Rohini has been working on this project for two weeks. She needs to complete the final report in the next 10 days.
C) Rohini have been working on this project for two weeks. She need to complete the final report in the next 10 days.
D) Rohini has been working on this project for two weeks. She need to complete the final report in the next 10 days.
e: The grammatically correct sentence is B. The error in sentence A is in the subject-verb agreement. "Rohini" is a singular subject, so the verb should be singular ("has") instead of the plural "have." The error in sentence C is again related to subject-verb agreement. "Have" [plural] should be replaced with the singular "has" to agree with the singular subject "Rohini." Additionally, "need" (plural) should be replaced with the singular "needs" to match the singular subject "She." The error in sentence D is in the subject-verb agreement. "She" (a singular subject) requires "needs" (singular) instead of the plural "need." Hence, (a) is the correct answer. NOTE: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: It is often observed in the animal kingdom
that the mother will fiercely protect its
e: The Correct Ans is - Option (C).Replace “offsprings” with “offspring”.Rule / Concept: Nouns with Identical Singular and Plural Forms- Certain nouns in English, such as Offspring, Deer, Sheep, Fish, and Apparatus, do not change their spelling to indicate plurality. They maintain the same form whether they refer to one individual or many. Adding an 's' to "offspring" is a common grammatical error, as the word "offspring" is already sufficient to represent multiple children or young ones.In this sentence, the context implies that a mother animal protects her young (plural). The examiner has added an 's' to "offspring" to create the plural "offsprings." According to the rule of identical forms, this is incorrect. The plural of offspring is simply offspring.Corrected Sentence - It is often observed in the animal kingdom that the mother will fiercely protect its offspring from any potential predators.REMEMBER THE LIST - Some nouns that have same singular and plural forms:- Deer, Sheep, Fish, Species, Series, Aircraft, Vacation, Offspring, Issue, Whereabouts, Headquarters.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error. 
The author and the publisher was thrilled with the overwhelming positive reception of their latest book, which quickly became a bestseller.
o: positive reception of their latest book,
e: The subject "The author and the publisher" is made up of two different individuals: "the author" and "the publisher." When two singular nouns are joined by "and", each having a preceding 'the', they form a compound subject, which is considered plural. Therefore, the verb should be in the plural form "were" instead of the singular form "was." Hence, (b) is the correct answer. Note: A compound subject is a subject in a sentence that consists of two or more nouns, pronouns, or noun phrases joined by a coordinating conjunction (such as "and" or "or") that share the same verb. The correct sentence: The author and the publisher were thrilled with the overwhelming positive reception of their latest book, which quickly became a bestseller.

t:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'
In practice rounds, my caddie, Greg, /and me works on my short/ game with a baseball glove.
o: and me works on my short
In practice rounds, my caddie, Greg,
e:
There is are two errors in the part in option (a). First, we need to replace the objective pronoun 'me' with subjective pronoun 'I' as it is the part of the subject of the sentence.
Also, the subject 'Greg and I' is plural in nature. So, singular verb 'works' should be replaced with plural verb 'work'.
Hence, option (a) is the answer.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: the village huts need to strengthen.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “to strengthen” with “strengthening” or “to be strengthened”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Passive Voice with "Need" When the subject of a sentence is the receiver of the action (usually a non-living thing), the verb "Need" must be followed by a structure that conveys a passive meaning. You have two grammatically correct choices to express that something requires an action to be done to it: Need + Gerund (V{ing}): This is an active form that carries a passive meaning. Need + Passive Infinitive (to + be + V3): This is the formal passive structure. 💢 Application to the Given Question "...the thatched roofs... need to strengthen." In this sentence, the "thatched roofs" are the subject. A roof cannot perform the act of strengthening itself; someone else must strengthen it. Therefore, the active infinitive "to strengthen" is incorrect. To fix the error, you must use either the gerund "strengthening" or the passive infinitive "to be strengthened." Corrected Sentence Since the monsoon season is approaching, the thatched roofs of the village huts need strengthening (or need to be strengthened). More Examples for Clarity Example 1 ✅ The car needs washing. (OR: needs to be washed). Example 2 ✅ My hair needs cutting. (OR: needs to be cut). Example 3 ✅ This software needs updating. (OR: needs to be updated).

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
e: Correction: Replace “better” with “the better”.Rule/Concept: The + Comparative (Gradual Increase/Decrease) – According to the provided notes, the definite article 'the' is used with a comparative degree in cases of gradual increase or decrease. This specific structure is used to show a parallel relationship where one action or state directly impacts another.Parallel Structure: The sentence links the amount of study (increase) with the level of understanding (increase).

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: After the successful completion of the project,
each other for their collective hard work.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C). Replace “each other” with “one another”.Rule / Concept: Reciprocal Pronouns (Each other vs. One another)-Each other: Used when referring to two persons or things.-One another: Used when referring to more than two persons or things.Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the subject is "all the department members." In a professional or organizational context, a "department" implies a group of multiple people (more than two) unless specified otherwise. Furthermore, the use of "all" and "collective" strongly indicates a plural group exceeding two. Therefore, the reciprocal pronoun must be "one another" instead of "each other."

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
<u>The patient</u> <u>had been waiting</u> patiently <u>for over two hours</u> before the doctor <u>finally attends</u> to him for a check-up.
e: The error is in the verb tense in the segment "finally attends". The first part of the sentence uses the Past Perfect Continuous tense (had been waiting), which describes an action that was ongoing for a duration before another event in the past. This sets the entire context of the sentence in the past. The second action must also be in the past tense. The verb 'attends' is in the Simple Present tense, which is incorrect. It should be in the Simple Past tense ('attended') to maintain the correct sequence of tenses. Correct sentence: The patient had been waiting patiently for over two hours before the doctor finally attended to him for a check-up. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. 
Jahangir is (A)/ considered as (B)/ the greatest among (C)/ the Mughal rulers (D).
e:
Part B has an error. Adverb 'as' can be used with 'regard, describe, define, treat, view'. But it cannot be used with verbs like 'name, elect, think, call, make, choose, consider'.
The correct sentence is: Jahangir is considered the greatest among the Mughal rulers.
Hence, the correct answer is option (d).

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error. 
The project has been progressing steadily for last summer, marked by significant milestones achieved by our dedicated team.
e: The error is in segment (b) "steadily for last summer." The phrase "for last summer" is incorrect because "last summer" refers to a time in the past. The correct expression should use "since" to indicate the starting point of the progress. "For" is rather used to show a period of time, in the past, present or future. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. The corrected sentence: The project has been progressing steadily since last summer, marked by significant milestones achieved by our dedicated team.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Most of the purified drinking water from reservoirs
stored in those rusted old iron metal tanks
were reported to be contaminated with toxic lead.
e: The Correct Ans is - Option (C)The plural verb "were" must be replaced with the singular verb "was."Rule/Concept: "Most of / Some of" with Uncountable Nouns Words like Most of, Some of, All of, and A lot of are "transparent" connectors. The verb does not look at these words; it looks strictly at the noun that follows the preposition "of".The Logic: If the noun is Uncountable (water, milk, furniture, information), the verb must be Singular.Logic Breakdown:Option (A): The head noun following "of" is "water." Water is an uncountable noun and requires a singular verb. (Word count: 8)Option (B): This segment acts as a distractor. It contains the plural words "reservoirs" and "tanks" right before the verb to make the plural agreement sound natural. (Word count: 8)Option (C): The verb "were" is plural. Because it must agree with the singular/uncountable "water," it must be changed to the singular "was." (Word count: 8)Correct Sentence: Most of the purified drinking water from reservoirs stored in those rusted old iron metal tanks was reported to be contaminated with toxic lead.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. 
All member of this / old age home actively / participates in the marathons / conducted by the state.
e: A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in person, number, and gender. The noun following 'all' is 'member' which is singular in nature. And 'all' refers to a complete group of people/things (plural in nature). So, instead of 'all', 'every' fits in the sentence as it refers to each member of the group individually (singular in nature). This means 'all' in the given sentence makes it grammatically incorrect. t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: to protect the wetlands since the new
industrial policy was proposed last year.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “worked” with “has been working”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Present Perfect Continuous with 'Since' When an action starts at a specific point in the past and continues up to the present moment, we must use the Present Perfect Continuous The word "Since" is a major indicator of this tense. It marks the starting point of the action. 💢 Application to the Given Question "The environmental organization worked... since the new industrial policy was proposed..." The Starting Point: The policy was proposed (Simple Past - V2). The Ongoing Action: The organization's work started then and is still happening because the sentence uses "since." The Error: By using "worked," the sentence implies the organization stopped working. Since the effort is ongoing in response to the policy, it must be "has been working." Corrected Sentence The environmental organization has been working tirelessly to protect the wetlands since the new industrial policy was proposed last year.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: When the CEO announced the sudden layoffs without any prior notice,
a sense of deep resentment and anxiety was emerged among the
long-term employees who had dedicated their entire careers to the firm.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) - Remove “was”.📌 Rule / Concept: Intransitive Verbs and the Passive Voice Trap -Certain verbs in English are Intransitive, meaning they do not take a direct object. Because they cannot "act upon" something else, they cannot be used in the Passive Voice. Common intransitive verbs frequently tested in SSC/Banking include: Occur, Happen, Emerge, Disappear, Appear, Arrive, Die, Exist.In the Passive Voice (be + V3), the subject receives the action. However, since these verbs represent things that simply "take place" or "become visible" on their own, using them in the passive form (was occurred, was emerged, will be happened) is a major grammatical error.💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the verb "emerge" is intransitive. The "sense of resentment" is the thing that is doing the emerging; it is not being "emerged" by someone else. Therefore, the helping verb "was" must be removed to keep the sentence in the Active Voice. More Examples for Clarity - Example 1: The accident occurred at midnight. (Not: was occurred)Example 2: A strange figure appeared in the doorway. (Not: was appeared)Example 3: What happened to your car? (Not: was happened)

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
e:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).Replace “are considering” with “consider”📌 Rule / Concept: Stative VerbsStative Nature of "Consider": The verb consider (when it means "to hold an opinion" or "to believe") is a stative verb. Stative verbs describe states that are generally constant, not actions that are happening at a specific moment. Therefore, they are rarely used in the continuous (-ing) form. 💢 Application to the Given Question - By using "are considering," the sentence implies that the Hindus are currently in the process of thinking about whether the Ganga is holy, as if they might change their minds tomorrow. Since this is a deep-seated, permanent religious belief, the continuous tense is logically and grammatically incorrect. It must be in the Simple Present: "consider."
 REMEMBER THE LIST of Stative verbs:- Think, Believe, Consider, Have, Own, Possess, Look, Seem, Appear, Consist, Contain, Comprise, Feel, Smell, Taste, Sound, Know, Resemble, Like, Love, Want, Agree, Hate, Forgive, Forget, Remember, Depend, Exist etc.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Despite the torrential downpour and the slippery track
conditions, the seasoned marathon runners performed
extreme well during the final grueling lap of the race.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “extreme” with “extremely”. Rule / Concept: Adverbs of Degree An Adjective describes a noun or a pronoun, whereas an Adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. In this context, when we want to intensify an adverb (like "well") or an adjective, we must use an Adverb of Degree Application to the Given Question "...performed extreme well during the final grueling lap..." In this sentence, "well" is an adverb modifying the verb "performed." To describe the extent or degree to which they performed well, we need another adverb ("extremely") to modify the adverb "well." Using the adjective "extreme" to modify an adverb is grammatically incorrect in formal examination standards. Corrected Sentence Despite the torrential downpour and the slippery track conditions, the seasoned marathon runners performed extremely well during the final grueling lap of the race More Examples for Clarity Example 1: The sun was extremely bright today. ✅ Example 2: She handled the pressure exceptionally well. ✅ Incorrect Usage Wrong example 1: He is a real talented singer. (Correct: really) ❌ Wrong example 2: The water was bitter cold. (Correct: bitterly) ❌ Things to Remember / Exam Tips The "LY" Test: When you see a word modifying an action or another descriptive word, check if it needs an "-ly" ending. Verb of Sensation Trap: Do not confuse these with verbs like feel, look, smell, sound, taste, which take adjectives (e.g., "She looks beautiful," not "beautifully"). Adverb modifying Adverb: Always remember the hierarchy: Adverb → Adverb → Verb. (e.g., He ran [Adv] extremely [Adv] fast [Verb-modifier]).

t:
Select the option that arranges the given words to form a grammatically correct and meaningful sentence.
The students eagerly their awaited results.
o: The awaited eagerly results their students.
Eagerly awaited the students their results.
The students eagerly awaited their results.
The students their eagerly awaited results.
e:
The subject 'the students' is correctly placed. 
The verb and the object of the sentence are not correctly placed. 
'Their results' forms the object of the sentence. 'Their' (the possessive adjective) should be used adjacent to the noun. 
The verb 'awaited' should be used adjacent to the adverb 'eagerly' that modifies it. 
So, the correct sentence is: The students eagerly awaited their results.
Hence, option (c) is the answer.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Maruti likes / adventure / stories, especially / an adventures of Tarzan.
e: The segment that contains a grammatical error is 'an adventures of Tarzan'. The error is the incorrect use of the article "an" before the word "adventures." The word "adventures" is a plural noun, referring to multiple adventures of Tarzan. Indefinite articles "a" or "an" are typically used before singular nouns, not plural nouns. Therefore, using "an" before "adventures" is grammatically incorrect because "an" is typically used before singular nouns, whereas "adventures" is a plural noun. The definite article "the" can be used before the noun "adventures" to imply that Maruti likes adventure stories in general, but has a particular fondness for the specific adventures of Tarzan. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. NOTE: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

high-stakes client meeting without any prior notice.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “him” with “his”.📌 Rule / Concept: Possessive Case before a Gerund - A Gerund is a verb ending in -ing that functions as a noun. Because it acts as a noun, the word that modifies it must be a possessive adjective (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) or a possessive noun (Ram's, Manager's).In formal grammar, you aren't annoyed by the "person" (him); you are annoyed by the "action" (his arriving).Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "arriving" is a gerund acting as the object of the preposition "by." The manager isn't necessarily annoyed by the man himself, but specifically by the act of his arrival being late. Therefore, the objective pronoun "him" must be changed to the possessive adjective "his.Corrected Sentence - The regional manager was understandably annoyed by his arriving late for the high-stakes client meeting without any prior notice. t:

o: One must do once duty proparly.
One must do ones duty properly.
One must do one's duti proprly.

e:
In the given sentence, when using the pronoun "one," the possessive form is "one's," not "his/her." Proparly: Incorrect spelling; the correct word is "properly."
One must do once duty proparly: Incorrect; "once" is wrong (should be "one's"), and "proparly" is misspelled. Negated due to multiple errors.
One must do ones duty properly: Incorrect; "ones" lacks the possessive apostrophe ("one's"). Negated as it is grammatically incorrect.
One must do one's duti proprly: Incorrect; "duti" and "proprly" are misspelled. Negated due to spelling errors.
One must do one's duty properly: Correctly uses "one's" and spells "properly" correctly.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Rohan is the only one of
e:
The Correct Ans is Option (b) Replace “remember” with “remembers”.

📌 Rule / Concept: The "Only One of" Rule

While the phrase "one of the" usually takes a plural verb (as seen in previous question), the addition of the word "only" changes the entire grammatical structure.

One of the + Plural Noun + Who/That : Plural Verb

The ONLY one of the + Plural Noun + Who/That : Singular Verb

In this specific structure, the relative pronoun (who/that) no longer refers to the plural group; it refers back to the singular word "one." Therefore, the verb must be singular.

Application to the Given Question - Because the sentence uses "the only one," the relative pronoun "who" is restricted to referring only to Rohan (the one). In English, singular subjects take singular verbs. For a verb in the present simple tense, a singular subject requires the addition of an 's' or 'es'. Thus, "remember" (plural) must be changed to "remembers" (singular).

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

-The "Only" Spotlight: Think of the word "only" as a spotlight. It moves the focus away from the "survivors" (the crowd) and shines it directly on "Rohan" (the individual).

-Verb Suffix: Remember the basic rule: Singular Noun + Verb with 's'. (He remembers / They remember).

-Scanning Strategy: When you see "One of the" in an exam, look for "Only." If "Only" is present, the verb at the end of the sentence must be singular.

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The journey through the <u>dense, unexplored jungle</u> was <u>more harder than the</u> experienced <u>adventurers had initially</u> <u>anticipated it</u>.
e: The error is in the segment "more harder than the". "Harder" is already the comparative form of the adjective "hard". Adding "more" before "harder" creates a double comparative, which is grammatically incorrect. The correct comparative form is simply "harder". Correct sentence: The journey through the dense, unexplored jungle was harder than the experienced adventurers had initially anticipated it. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: · The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made. The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared. The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared. ("Hard" is positive, "harder" is comparative, "hardest" is superlative. "More harder" is an incorrect formation of the comparative degree.)

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error
o: The local distributor confirmed that they supplied
Four dozens pencils and five dozens notebooks
to the primary school located in the suburban district.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “four dozens” with “four dozen” AND “five dozens” with “five dozen”.Rule / Concept: Nouns of Measurement with Definite NumeralsWhen nouns like dozen, score, hundred, thousand, million, and billion are preceded by a definite numeral (e.g., one, two, four, five, several), they are used in their singular form.-Structure 1 (Definite): Numeral + Singular Noun (Dozen/Hundred) + Plural Noun.-Structure 2 (Indefinite): Plural Noun (Dozens/Hundreds) + of + Plural NounApplication to the Given Question - In this sentence, the words "dozen" are preceded by the definite numerals four and five. According to the rule, when a specific number is mentioned, the unit of measurement (dozen) must remain singular. You only use the plural "dozens" if the specific number is removed and followed by "of" (e.g., dozens of pencils)Corrected Sentence - The local distributor confirmed that they supplied four dozen pencils and five dozen notebooks to the primary school located in the suburban district.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The young entrepreneur will buy a sprawling bungalow
in the heart of South Delhi next month as he
has already paid the token amount to the builder.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A). Replace “will buy” with “is buying”.📌 Rule / Concept: Planned Personal Future Actions- We distinguish between Fixed Official Schedules (Simple Present) and Planned Personal/Unofficial Actions.When an individual has made a firm personal arrangement (such as paying a token amount, booking tickets, or fixing a date) for an action occurring in the near future, the Present Continuous Tense (is/am/are + V{ing}) is preferred over the Future Indefinite (will + V1). This is because "will" often denotes a spontaneous decision, whereas "is/am/are + ing" confirms a pre-decided plan. 💢 Application to the Given Question - The sentence provides a clear context: the action of buying is planned and certain because the "token amount" has already been paid. This makes it a firm personal arrangement rather than a vague future possibility. Therefore, according to the rule of planned future actions, "will buy" should be replaced with "is buying". More Examples for Clarity- Example 1 ✅: I am meeting the doctor at 5 PM today. (Already have an appointment).Example 2 ✅: We are shifting to our new apartment next Sunday. (Everything is packed).Example 3 ✅: They are organizing a charity event next week. (Venue is booked).

e: The part that contains the error is 'since'. The phrase "since six days" is incorrect because "since" is used to specify a starting point in time or an event that continues up to the present. It does not convey the duration of time worked by the volunteers. The preposition "for" is used to indicate a duration of time. Therefore, the correct phrase should be "for six days," which correctly communicates the duration of time during which the volunteers worked tirelessly to build homes for the underprivileged community. Hence, (c) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: The volunteers worked tirelessly for six days to build homes for the underprivileged community. NOTE: "A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples I. The teacher scolded the child for being late. II. We're going to a party. · The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition. · The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object."

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “cancelled” with “cancel”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Bare Infinitives after "Had better" The phrase "Had better" is a modal idiom used to give strong advice or to indicate what is a desirable or necessary action in a specific situation. Regardless of the fact that it contains the word "had" (which usually signals the past tense), it refers to the present or future. It must always be followed by a Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to"). Using a Past Participle (V3), a Past Tense verb (V2), or a Full Infinitive (to + V1) after "had better" is a common grammatical error. 💢 Application to the Given Question "...you had better cancelled your trip." In this sentence, "had better" is used to provide advice regarding the weather. The verb following "had better" is "cancelled" (the past participle form). According to the rule, this must be in the base form. Therefore, "cancelled" must be changed to "cancel". REMEMBER: Use bare infinitives after these ; Had better/ Had rather / Would better/ Would rather corrected Sentence Considering the rapidly deteriorating weather conditions in the mountains, you had better cancel your trip.

If the relative pronoun already represents the object, adding a personal pronoun (like him, her, it, them) to serve as that same object creates a grammatical redundancy called a "double object."KEY RULE: NO OF SUBJECT=NO OF VERB (Always check )Application to the Given Question"had tracked him across several international borders"In this sentence, "whom" is the relative pronoun acting as the object of the verb "tracked." t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: We reasoned that individuals who had frequent indigestion would report
especially high tendencies to experience intolerance to nuts,

📌 Rule / Concept: Reported Reasoning + Past Hypothetical Outcome (Third Conditional Logic)

When a sentence reports past reasoning, assumption, or inference about outcomes that were also expected in the past, the correct modal structure is: would have + past participle

This reflects an unreal or speculative past result, not a general or present tendency.

💢 Application to the Given Question

“We reasoned that …”


 Past reporting verb → fixes the reasoning in the past


“…individuals who had frequent indigestion …”


 Past condition/state


Therefore, the logically expected outcome must also belong to the past hypothetical frame:


 would have reported ✅

 shifts the meaning toward a present/general tendency
 breaks tense and conditional consistency

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Hardly he attended the weekly strategy briefings
during his tenure as the project manager, which eventually
led to several critical lapses in the final execution of the plan.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “he attended” with “did he attend”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion with Adverb of Frequency (Hardly) When a sentence begins with a negative adverb of frequency like Hardly, Scarcely, or Barely, the sentence must follow the rule of Partial Inversion. Even if the sentence is a simple statement about a habit or a past action (and not part of the "Hardly... when" conjunction pair), the auxiliary verb must come before the subject. If the sentence is in the Simple Past tense (like "attended"), we must use the auxiliary verb "did" and change the main verb to its base form. 💢 Application to the Given Question Hardly he attended the weekly strategy briefings... In this sentence, the word "Hardly" is used at the beginning for emphasis. The verb "attended" is in the Simple Past. To satisfy the rule of inversion, we must introduce the auxiliary verb "did" before the subject "he" and change "attended" to its base form "attend". Corrected Sentence Hardly did he attend the weekly strategy briefings during his tenure as the project manager, which eventually led to several critical lapses in the final execution of the plan.

Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error.
The collection of sculptures is displayed on the museum, showcasing rare and historical pieces from different eras and cultures.
o: The collection of sculptures is displayed
e:
The error lies in the preposition "on" in the phrase "on the museum." The preposition "on" typically indicates placement on top of a surface, such as "on the table" or "on the wall." In this case, sculptures are not physically placed on the museum building. Instead, they are displayed within the museum's interior space.
Use "in" to indicate that the collection is inside the museum, where the sculptures are being exhibited. This is the most appropriate option since sculptures are displayed within the space of the museum.
"At" can also be used when you want to refer to a specific location, like a building or venue, without focusing on whether it's inside or outside. Example: "The collection of sculptures is displayed at the museum."
So, the correct sentence is: The collection of sculptures is displayed in/at the museum, showcasing rare and historical pieces from different eras and cultures.
Hence, option (b) is the answer.

t:
The following sentence has been split into three segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If the sentence is error free, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The seat of new staff was filled/ by an old craftsman/ who had an extensible knowledge of prehistoric designs and crafts.
o: who had an extensible knowledge of prehistoric designs and crafts
The seat of new staff was filled
e:
'Extensive' will replace 'extensible'. Extensible means capable of being extended. 'Extensive' means thorough; dealing with a wide range of information. The person is chosen because of his 'thorough knowledge of craftsmanship' which is helpful for the job. So, 'extensive' is the right word.
Hence, option (b) is correct.

The
following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the
segment that contains a grammatical error.
e: Use of apostrophe with Sachin is incorrect here. Sachin and Sehwag's partnership will be the correct usage as the century is made in partnership.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: sternly asked the witness what was he
doing near the crime scene that night.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “what was he” with “what he was”.📌 Rule / Concept: Word Order in Indirect Questions -When a question is asked directly, we use the Interrogative Word Order (Wh-word + Auxiliary + Subject). However, when a question is embedded within a statement or reported in indirect speech, it loses its interrogative nature and follows the Assertive Word Order (Wh-word + Subject + Auxiliary).💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the question is being reported by the prosecutor (Indirect Speech). Because the sentence is now a statement describing an inquiry, the inversion of the subject ("he") and the verb ("was") must be undone. The auxiliary verb "was" should follow the subject "he."

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Sameer is working in an IT firm in Pune for the past six years.
e:
“Has been working” will replace “is working” because the event started in the past and is still continuing. Hence, Present Perfect Continuous Tense will be used.
So, there is an error in option a).
Hence, option a) is correct.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The ancient mansion at the edge of the forest feels eerily
quiet and deserted in the dim glow of the evening, with
creaking floors and shadowy corners making visitors uneasy.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A).Replace “eerily” with nothing or use “eerie” if needed.Rule/Concept: Verbs of SensationVerbs of sensation (look, feel, smell, taste, sound) describe the state or quality of a noun.They must be followed by adjectives, not adverbs.Using an adverb like eerily after a sensation verb is incorrect.Corrected Sentence -✓ The ancient mansion at the edge of the forest feels eerie and deserted in the dim glow of the evening, with creaking floors and shadowy corners making visitors uneasy.More Examples for Clarity -The cake tastes sweet. (Not “tastes sweetly”). The music sounds beautiful. (Not “sounds beautifully”). The flowers smell fragrant. (Not “smell fragrantly”).

t: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
o: Rajat have been working on this project for two weeks.
Rajat has been working on this project for two weeks.
Rajat has been working on this project since two weeks.
Rajat have been working on this project since two weeks.
e: The sentence given in option (b) is grammatically correct. Options (a) and (d) are incorrect because of the subject-verb agreement issue. The subject "Rajat" is singular, so the correct verb form should be the singular "has" instead of plural "have". Option (c) is also incorrect. The phrase "since two weeks" is incorrect. The word "since" is used to refer to a specific point in time when an action started. It is typically followed by a specific point in time (e.g., since Monday, since June). It is not used to indicate a duration of time like "two weeks". The correct preposition to use here is "for". "For" is used to indicate the duration of time something has been happening. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: Rajat has been working on this project for two weeks. NOTE: A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples I. The teacher scolded the child for being late. II. We're going to a party. · The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition. · The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object. Subject-verb agreement means that a subject and its verb must be both singular or both plural: A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. For example, in the sentence 'John lives in France', the subject John (singular 'he') 'agrees with' the third person singular form of the verb to live - lives.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Being an oldest member of the club, / he was often consulted by others / for his valuable advice and experience.
o: for his valuable advice and experience
Being an oldest member of the club,
he was often consulted by others
e: The error is in the part "Being an oldest member of the club,". "Oldest" is a superlative adjective.
