Superlative adjectives are usually preceded by the definite article "the" because they indicate a unique item or person in a group. "An" (indefinite article) is incorrect here. Correct Sentence: Being the oldest member of the club, he was often consulted by others for his valuable advice and experience. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: · Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles. Superlative adjectives (like "oldest") generally require the definite article "the." · The Superlative degree: Indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

Her remarkable decision to pursue advanced medical studies abroad / was met with strong approve and unwavering support / from her entire family and close friends.
o: Her remarkable decision to pursue advanced medical studies abroad
was met with strong approve and unwavering support
from her entire family and close friends
e: The error is in part (b) with the word "approve." "Strong" is an adjective that should modify a noun. "Approve" is a verb. The noun form needed here, parallel to "unwavering support" (adjective + noun), is "approval." Correct Sentence: Her remarkable decision to pursue advanced medical studies abroad was met with strong approval and unwavering support from her entire family and close friends. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: · Parts of Speech: Understanding the different roles words play (noun, verb, adjective, adverb, etc.) is crucial for correct sentence construction. · Parallelism: In grammar, parallelism, also known as parallel structure or parallel construction, is a balance within one or more sentences of similar phrases or clauses that have the same grammatical structure. Here, "strong approval" and "unwavering support" maintain parallel structure (adjective + noun). · Abstract Noun: It is the name given to ideas, qualities, and conditions - things that cannot be seen or touched and things which have no physical reality. "Approval" and "support" are abstract nouns.

t:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. Identify the part that has an error. Select the option that has an error.
The professor <u>instructed</u> the students <u>to submit their</u> final essays <u>to their teaching assistant and myself</u> by the <u>end of the day.</u>
o: to their teaching assistant and myself
e: This question tests the incorrect use of a reflexive pronoun. "Myself" should only be used reflexively (I hurt myself) or for emphasis (I myself will do it). It cannot be used as an object in a prepositional phrase. The correct objective pronoun is "me." The correct phrasing is "...to their teaching assistant and me." Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

t: In the following question, four sentences are given that may or may not have grammatical errors. Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct and mark it as your answer. If all the sentences are incorrect, choose 'All are incorrect' as your answer.
o: The principal's assistant's son's is looking for his wallet.
The average weight of the class are sixty-five kilograms.
e:
Only sentence (b) is grammatically correct. In sentence (b), 'two' and 'two' are compounded as a plural noun and the use of the plural verb 'make' is the correct form of verb that is to be used. But, in the sentence (a), the possessive form of the noun 'son's' is incorrect as the possessive form must follow a noun to denote the possession, which is not the case in the sentence. In sentence (c), the collective quantity 'kilograms' is treated as a plural noun, which is incorrect and in sentence (d), the noun that ends with the word 's', 'news' is treated as a plural noun and plural verb is incorrectly used in the sentence. 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb after it. So, 'are' should be replaced with 'is'.
Hence, the correct answer is option (b).
The correct sentences are:
The principal's assistant's son is looking for his wallet.
The average weight of the class is sixty-five kilograms.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The hen had lain several eggs
in the corner of the barn before
e: The Correct Ans is Option (A). Replace “lain” with “laid”.📌 Rule/Concept: Transitive vs. Intransitive Verbs (Lie vs. Lay) -The confusion arises because the past tense of "Lie" is "Lay." However, they are two distinct verbs:Lie (Intransitive): To recline or be in a flat position. It does not take an object.Forms: Lie (V1), Lay (V2), Lain (V3), Lying (V-ing).Lay (Transitive): To put or place something down. It must have an object.Forms: Lay (V1), Laid (V2), Laid (V3), Laying (V-ing).Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "several eggs" is the direct object receiving the action of being placed or produced. Therefore, we must use the transitive verb Lay. Since the sentence uses the past perfect tense ("had" + V3), we need the V3 form of "Lay," which is Laid. "Lain" is the V3 of the intransitive verb "Lie" (to recline), which is incorrect here.More Examples for Clarity -1- He laid his coat on the bed. (Object: coat)2- I have lain on this sofa for three hours. (No object; reclining) 3- Please lay the book on the shelf. (Object: book).Things to Remember / Exam Tips -Object Check: If there is a noun/pronoun after the verb (eggs, stress, foundation, book), use Lay/Laid/Laid.The V3 Trap: Remember that Lain is for resting/reclining, and Laid is for putting/placing.Action Type: "Lay" requires an actor putting something somewhere. "Lie" describes the state of the subject itself.

t:
Spot the erroneous part if any, in the following sentence.
The plumber/ <u>fixed the leak</u> (A)/ <u>after the water</u> (B)/ <u>had flood</u> (C)/ the basement. / No error (D).
e: The erroneous part in the sentence is (C). The error in segment (C) relates to the verb tense agreement. The sentence describes two past actions: the flooding of the basement and the plumber fixing the leak. The sequence of events indicates that the flooding occurred before the plumber fixed the leak. To express this sequence of events properly, the past perfect tense is used to indicate an action that occurred before another past action. In this case, "had flooded" (past participle form (V3)) should be used instead of "had flood" (flood is the base form of the verb) to convey that the flooding happened prior to the plumber fixing the leak. Hence, (c) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: "The plumber fixed the leak after the water had flooded the basement."

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: After the severe hailstorm damaged the
warehouse roof, the manager got the entire
structure repair by a team of specialized contractors.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “repair” with “repaired”. 📌 Rule / Concept: The Causative Passive Sub + get/have + object + past participle + by + real doer When we use verbs like Have or Get to show that someone else performed a task for us, the grammar depends entirely on what follows the verb. If a thing/object (the receiver) comes first, we must use the Past Participle (V3). The Logic: Active: The manager got the contractors (People) to repair the roof. Passive: The manager got the roof (Object) repaired. In the passive version, we don't care who did it as much as what was done to the object. 💢 Application to the Given Question The sentence is designed to overwhelm you with descriptive clauses ("After the severe hailstorm," "team of specialized contractors"), but the core error is found in the causative link: "...got the entire structure (Object) repair (Incorrect Verb Form)..." The Causative Verb: "Got" The Object: "The entire structure" (The warehouse roof/building). The Action: "Repair." Since the "structure" cannot repair itself, the relationship is passive. the verb "repair" must be changed to its third form, "repaired." Corrected sentence After the severe hailstorm damaged the warehouse roof, the manager got the entire structure repaired by a team of specialized contractors. More Examples for Clarity Example 1: I had my hair cut yesterday. (Not cutted or to cut). Example 2: She got her laptop fixed at the service center. (Not fix). Example 3: You should have your eyes tested regularly. (Not test).

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: If I were in charge of the last project
I would have delegated a little more
e:
Option A — replace “were” with “had been”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Third Conditional (Unreal Past Condition)

This sentence refers to:


 a completed project in the past
 a hypothetical situation contrary to fact


The correct conditional structure for unreal past situations is:

If + had been / had + V³ → would have + V³

💢 Application to the Given Question

“the last project”


 Clearly refers to a finished past event
 Hence, the condition must be located in the past unreal


“would have delegated”


 Correct third-conditional result form
 Already fixed in the past hypothetical frame


Therefore:


 if I had been in charge ✅
 if I were in charge ❌ (this form is for unreal present, not unreal past)


Since the result clause is already correct, the only error lies in Part A.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Despite the government's best efforts to
contain the virus, the infection had spreaded
to the neighboring districts within a week.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “spreaded” with “spread”📌Rule/Concept: Irregular Verbs with Identical Forms- These verbs have same V1/V2/V3 :- Wed, Cost, Set, Bet, Bid, Thrust, Hit, Cut, Slit, Spread, Read, Burst, Quit, Shut, Shed, Rid, Cast, Telecast, Broadcast, Overcast, Forecast, etc.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Despite the widespread implementation of several modern farming techniques and
subsidies, the peasantry of this drought-stricken region is still struggling
to repay the high-interest loans taken from local moneylenders.
e: The Correct Ans is - Option (B). Replace “is” with “are”.Rule/Concept: Nouns Singular in Form but Plural in Meaning - Certain collective nouns such as Peasantry, Gentry, Clergy, Poultry, Cattle, and Police - do not end in ‘s’, yet they represent a group or class of individuals. These nouns are always considered plural and must be followed by a plural verb. In this context, "Peasantry" refers to the class of small farmers or agricultural laborers as a whole. Although it appears singular in form (lacking an 's'), it refers to a collective group of people. Therefore, the singular auxiliary verb "is" is grammatically incorrect. It must be replaced with the plural verb "are" to achieve proper subject-verb agreementCorrected Sentence - Despite the widespread implementation of several modern farming techniques and subsidies, the peasantry of this drought-stricken region are still struggling to repay the high-interest loans taken from local moneylenders.LIST: Some nouns that look singular but are plural:- Cattle, Vermin, Police, Gentry, Peasantry, Children, People, Poultry, Cavalry, Clergy, Infantry etc.

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “trained”: Only highly trained officials were allowed to access the confidential records stored in the digital archive.
e: Answer: C) Participle/Adjective Explanation: A participle is a verb form that functions as an adjective. Past participles often end in -ed, -en, or irregular forms. Here, “trained” describes the noun “officials.” What kind of officials? → highly trained officials Since it describes the noun rather than acting as the main verb, “trained” functions as a participle (adjectival participle).

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: In light of the recent economic downturn,
the board of directors may likely postpone
the annual general meeting until the next quarter.
e: Replace “may likely postpone” with “may postpone” or “is likely to postpone”. Rule / Concept: Redundancy of Possibility - In English grammar, the modal verbs 'May' and 'Might' are used to express possibility or likelihood. Similarly, words like 'likely', 'possibly', 'probably', 'perhaps', and 'chance' also denote the same sense of uncertainty. Using a modal of possibility along with an adverb/adjective of possibility in the same clause is redundant (superfluous). You must use one or the other, but never both. Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "may" already indicates that the postponement is a possibility. Adding "likely" creates a "double possibility" error. To correct it, you should either say "may postpone" or "is likely to postpone." More Examples for Clarity It may rain tonight. ✔ It may possibly rain today. ❌ Things to Remember / Exam Tips The "May/Likely" Pair: This is a classic "Superfluous Expression" error frequently tested in SSC Mains. The "Can/Able" Parallel: Just as "Can + Able" is wrong, "May + Likely/Possibly" is wrong. Active vs. Passive: "Likely" often requires the "to + V1" structure (e.g., is likely to go), whereas "May" is followed directly by the base form of the verb (e.g., may go) Don't Over-correct: Students often get so used to spotting "Can be able to" errors that they start marking "May be able to" as an error too. Remember: Possibility (May) + Ability (Be able to) = Correct. It is used for future possibility based on present condition.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Kushi said/ that the sun/ rise in/ the east.
e: The part given in option (c) has the error. The plural verb "rise" cannot be used after the singular noun "sun". Replace "rise" with the singular verb "rises" to rectify the error. The correct sentence is: Kushi said that the sun rises in the east. Hence, the correct answer is option (c). Note: Direct and Indirect Speech: We use direct speech when we repeat someone's words and indirect speech when we use our own words to report what someone says. For Example: Direct speech: 'I like watching movies,' Seema said; Indirect speech: Seema said she likes watching movies.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Psychologists have observed that prolonged exposure to high levels of blue light
from digital screens can adversely effect the circadian rhythms of teenagers,
resulting in chronic sleep deprivation and a noticeable decline in academic performance.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “effect” with “affect”.📌 Rule / Concept: Affect vs. Effect Affect (Verb): To influence or produce a change in something. (e.g., "The weather affects my mood.")Effect (Noun): The result or consequence of a change. (e.g., "The weather had a strange effect on me." 💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, we need a verb to describe the action of blue light "influencing" or "altering" the circadian rhythms. Since the word follows the modal verb "can" and the adverb "adversely," it must be the verb affect. Using the noun "effect" here is grammatically incorrect.More Examples for Clarity - Example 1: The new law will affect everyone in the country. Example 2: The medicine had a soothing effect on the patient.Example 3: Does the noise affect your concentration?

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. The dining room is located interior with the living room, creating a cosy and integrated space for family gatherings.
e: According to the rule, the adjectives that end in 'ior' like 'senior, junior, interior, exterior, etc.' are followed by 'to'. So, 'interior to' is the correct phrase and not 'interior with'. The correct sentence is - "The dining room is located interior to the living room, creating a cosy and integrated space for family gatherings." Hence, option (d) is correct. NOTE/- Adjectives: Words which are used with a noun/pronoun to describe or point out, the person, animal, place, or thing which the noun names, or to tell the number or quantity, are called Adjectives.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Celebrated as one of the most dedicated surgeons in the hospital,
Dr. Mehta take charge of the emergency unit when
multiple accident victims arrived late at night.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “take” with “took”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Narrative Tense Consistency When a sentence describes a specific event that occurred in the past, all the main verbs related to that event must remain in the Simple Past Tense . If a sentence provides a time-marker in the past (such as "when... arrived"), it establishes a "Past Zone." 💢 Application to the Given Question "...Dr. Mehta take charge... when multiple accident victims arrived..." There are two related actions in this sentence: The victims arrived (Simple Past - $V_2$). Dr. Mehta take charge (Simple Present - $V_1$). The word "when" creates a direct temporal link between the two actions. Since the arrival of the victims happened in the past, the act of taking charge must also have happened at that same past moment. Therefore, "take" (Present) must be changed to "took" (Past) to match the narrative context. Corrected Sentence Celebrated as one of the most dedicated surgeons in the hospital, Dr. Mehta took charge of the emergency unit when multiple accident victims arrived late at night.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
Though the detective worked very hard / on this complex case / but he could not / solve the mystery.
o: Though the detective worked very hard
e: The conjunction 'though' (or 'although') is used to show a contrast between two clauses. The clause containing it is correctly followed by a comma, but not by 'but'. Using 'but' creates a redundancy because 'though' itself indicates the contrast. Correct sentence: Though the detective worked very hard on this complex case, he could not solve the mystery. So, there is an error in the part mentioned in option c). Hence, option (c) is the answer. Note: A conjunction (also called a connective) is a word such as and, because, but, for, if, or, when etc. Conjunctions are used to connect phrases, clauses, and sentences.

t:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
<u>It is high time</u> that the municipal corporation <u>realises</u> its responsibility <u>towards maintaining</u> <u>the cleanliness</u> of the city's public parks.
e: The error is in the verb tense in the segment "realises". The idiomatic expression "It is time" or "It is high time" is followed by a subject and a verb in the Simple Past tense. This structure is used to express that something should have been done earlier and is overdue. The verb realises is in the Simple Present tense. The correct verb form to use in this structure is the Simple Past tense, which is 'realised'. Correct sentence: It is high time that the municipal corporation realised its responsibility towards maintaining the cleanliness of the city's public parks. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The old librarian, who had worked at the public library for over forty years, / knew precisely where every book was shelved / and could often recommend the perfect read.
o: knew precisely where every book was shelved
and could often recommend the perfect read
The old librarian, who had worked at the public library for over forty years,
e:
The sentence is grammatically correct. All parts are grammatically sound and logically connected.
Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t:
The
following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the
segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: and the problem is that they
e:
The correct word should be "politicians", which is a plural noun. 
These + Plural Noun is the correct usage.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. 
The producer and director of the (A)/ film, Rahul Shah arrived at the hotel (B)/ yesterday and they are (C)/ eager to meet you. (D)
e:
Part C has an error. 
When two singular nouns are joined by 'and', and they refer to the same person or thing, the pronoun used must be singular in number. In this case, the definite article is placed before the first noun. So, the pronoun 'they are' is grammatically incorrect in the given sentence because it is a plural noun. It should be replaced with 'he is' to rectify the given sentence. 
Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: The producer and director of the film, Rahul Roy arrived at the hotel yesterday and he is eager to meet you.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
This was the man whom treated her so coldly earlier today.
e: The objective pronoun 'whom' is used to refer to objects. In the given sentence, 'the man' is the subject of the sentence and not the object. So, we should use the subjective pronoun 'who' in place of 'whom'. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: This was the man who treated her so coldly earlier today. Note: Subjective Pronouns: The pronouns I, you, we, he, she, it, and they are known as subjective pronouns because they act as the subjects of verbs: We went to the party. Objective Pronouns: The pronouns me, you, us, him, her, it, and them are called objective pronouns because they act as the objects of verbs and prepositions: Anjali drove us home.

t:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. Identify the part that has an error. Select the option that has an error.
<u>The board's mandate requires</u> that <u>each department head</u> <u>submits a detailed</u> quarterly <u>report to the oversight</u> committee.
e: This question tests the subjunctive mood. After verbs expressing a demand, request, or requirement (like "requires that," "insists that," "suggests that"), the following verb should be in its base form. The correct phrasing is "...that each department head submit..." not "submits." So, the correct sentence is: The board's mandate requires that each department head submit a detailed quarterly report to the oversight committee. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “since”: Since the weather conditions had deteriorated significantly during the night, the rescue team decided to postpone the expedition until further notice.
e: Answer: C) Conjunction Explanation: A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases, or clauses. A subordinating conjunction connects a dependent clause with an independent clause. Here, “since” introduces the dependent clause: “Since the weather conditions had deteriorated significantly during the night” It gives the reason for postponing the expedition. Since it connects two clauses, “since” functions as a subordinating conjunction.

t:
In the following question, a sentence is given which is divided into four parts. Out of the four parts, one part contains an error. Mark that option as your answer. 
Some money from the parents' (A)/ accounts are spent by (B)/ the 17-year-old to buy (C)/ in-game cosmetic items and virtual ammunition. (D)
e:
Part B has an error. 
When any of 'some, any, none, all, more / most, is used with a countable noun, the verb is plural and when any of these is used with an uncountable noun, the verb is singular. Since the noun 'money' is an uncountable noun, the verb 'are' should be replaced with its singular form 'is' to rectify the given sentence. 
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.
The correct sentence is: Some money from the parents' accounts is spent by the 17-year-old to buy in-game cosmetic items and virtual ammunition.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The logistics manager confirmed that the
freighter, which was laden with over two thousand
tons of hazardous chemicals, was ready to sail.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “laden” with “loaded”.📌 Rule / Concept: Loaded vs. Laden -Loaded (Functional/Mechanical): Used when a vehicle, container, or device is filled with a specific cargo or contents.Key Contexts: Trucks, ships, planes, guns, cameras, or even data.Example: The loaded gun was kept in the safe.Laden (Descriptive/Natural): Used to describe a state of being "weighed down" or heavily burdened. It carries a more literary or physical connotation of "hanging heavy."Key Contexts: Tree branches (fruit/snow), people (carrying bundles/bags), or abstract burdens (emotions/guilt).Example: The orchard was laden with ripe peaches.💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the object is a freighter (a cargo ship). Because a ship is a commercial vessel designed to carry a specific "load" of cargo (hazardous chemicals), the word "loaded" is the precise technical term required.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.
She will come to work though it doesn't rain tomorrow.
e: The segment that contains a grammatical error is 'though it doesn't'. The use of the conjunction "though" is inappropriate in the context of the sentence. "Though" is used to introduce a contrast or concession. However, in the sentence, there is no clear contrast being made. A more suitable conjunction for the given context would be "if", which implies a conditional relationship between the two clauses. The word "if" introduces a condition. It sets up a hypothetical situation where the action described in the main clause ("She will come to work") depends on whether the condition stated in the conditional clause ("it doesn't rain tomorrow") is fulfilled or not. Other segments of the sentence are grammatically correct. Hence, (d) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: She will come to work if it doesn't rain tomorrow. Note: "CONJUNCTIONS A conjunction (also called a connective) is a word such as and, because, but, for, if, or, when etc. Conjunctions are used to connect phrases, clauses, and sentences."

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The prodigy, who began his training at the age of four,
can play flute with such haunting beauty that the entire audience
often remains spellbound throughout the performance.
e: Rule/Concept: Use of 'The' with the names of Musical Instruments - The definite article 'the' is used before the names of musical instruments when they are referred to in a general sense or when someone is playing them (e.g., He plays the guitar).However, when musical instruments are referred to as countable objects (i.e., buying, selling, or owning a specific unit), 'a' or 'an' is used instead of 'the'.Corrected Sentence- The prodigy, who began his training at the age of four, can play the flute with such haunting beauty that the entire audience often remains spellbound throughout the performance.More Examples for Clarity-1. He has been learning the guitar since childhood. (Refers to the skill)2. I saw a guitar lying in the corner of the room. (Refers to a physical object)

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The paintings in this gallery are / often more impressive than the other museum / we visited during our trip last year.
o: often more impressive than the other museum
we visited during our trip last year
The paintings in this gallery are
e: The error is in the part "often more impressive than the other museum". This sentence attempts to compare "The paintings in this gallery" with "the other museum." This is a faulty comparison because paintings should be compared with other paintings, not with a museum. The comparison should be between "the paintings in this gallery" and "the paintings in the other museum" or "those in the other museum." Correct Sentence: The paintings in this gallery are often more impressive than those in the other museum we visited during our trip last year. (Or: ...than the paintings in the other museum...) Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: · Faulty Comparison (Logical Comparison): Comparisons must be made between like items. Here, artworks (paintings) should be compared with other artworks, not with an institution (museum). · Demonstrative pronouns: "Those" would be used as a demonstrative pronoun here to refer to "the paintings."

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. 
Equipments used for the extraction of / groundwater as well as / any combinations of such / structures is provided by the authority.
o: structures are provided by the authority
Equipments used for the extraction of
e:
The noun 'equipment' is an uncountable noun. So, we cannot make its plural form by adding s at the end. So, the noun 'equipments' should be replaced with 'equipment' to rectify the given sentence. Therefore, the error is in the part in option (d). 
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.
The correct sentence is: Equipment used for the extraction of groundwater as well as any combinations of such structures is provided by the authority.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
One can never imagine / how hot it gets in Delhi / unless one doesn't go/ there in person.
o: How hot it gets in Delhi
e: We use until as a subordinating conjunction to connect an action or an event to a point in time. Example: Let's wait here until the rain stops. So, 'unless' should be replaced with 'until'. Hence, option (b) is the answer. 'Unless' is similar in meaning to 'if not' and can be used instead of 'if not' in certain types of conditional sentences. The correct sentence is: One can never imagine how hot it gets in Delhi until one doesn't go there in person.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Had the whistle-blower not leaked the classified
documents to the press last winter, the corporate
fraud would remained hidden from the public eye.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) - Replace “would remained” with “would have remained”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Third Conditional (Inverted Form) The Third Conditional is used to express an unreal or hypothetical situation in the past and its probable past result. When the sentence begins with "Had" (inversion), it replaces the "If + had + V3" structure. The mandatory structure for the result clause is: Had + Subject + V3 (Past Participle) + ..., Subject + would/could/might + have + V3. 💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the condition is correctly established using "Had the whistle-blower not leaked..." (an unreal past condition). However, the result clause in Part C uses "would remained," which is grammatically incomplete. To show a past hypothetical result, "would" must be followed by "have" and the past participle (V3) "remained." More Examples for Clarity Example 1 ✅: Had I known about the traffic, I would have started earlier. Example 2 ✅: Had she studied harder, she might have passed the entrance exam. Example 3 ✅: The company could have avoided bankruptcy had it diversified its portfolio.

t:
Select the grammatically correct sentence. 

A. An engineer found a brilliant solution for the complex problem they encountered yesterday.
B. The engineer found a brilliant solution to the complex problem they encountered yesterday.
C. A engineer found a brilliant solution of the complex problem they encountered yesterday.
D. The engineer found a brilliant solution of the complex problem they encountered yesterday.
e: Sentence B correctly uses the collocation "solution to" and the article "an" appropriately. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. A & D- The phrase "solution for/of" is incorrect. The correct collocation is "solution to." C- "A engineer" is grammatically incorrect as "a" is used before the noun starting with a consonant sound, but "engineer" starts with a vowel sound. So, it should be "an engineer." Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option.
He stood on the (A)/ street corner, haranguing (B)/ passer-bys about the stupidity (C)/ of the forthcoming war. (D)
e:
Part C has an error. 
A compound noun forms plural by making the principal word plural. For example, 'Daughter-in-laws' is incorrect; the correct plural form of 'daughter-in-law' is 'daughters-in-law'. Similarly, the plural form of 'passer-by' (a person who happens to be going past something, especially on foot) is 'passers-by'. 
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: He stood on the street corner, haranguing passers-by about the stupidity of the forthcoming war.

t:
In the given sentence, several segments have been underlined. One of these underlined segments is grammatically incorrect in the context of its usage in the sentence. Identify the incorrect segment from the following options. 
Neither Ketan <u>nor his brother have</u> <u>attended the family gathering</u>, <u>as both are occupied with prior</u> <u>commitments and engagements elsewhere</u>.
o: as both are occupied with prior
e:
The subject "Neither Ketan nor his brother" is singular, so the correct verb form should be "has attended." We use a singular verb when the subject after "nor" is singular and a plural verb when the subject after "nor" is plural. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.
The final correct sentence would be: Neither Ketan nor his brother has attended the family gathering, as both are occupied with prior commitments and engagements elsewhere.

t: The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar. Despite having access to the most advanced satellite imagery, the rescue team _________ locate the wreckage due to the dense forest canopy and heavy cloud cover.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (b). Rule / Concept: Redundancy of Ability & Double Negatives – In English grammar, the negative form of the modal "can" is used to express present inability or impossibility. Two major traps are frequently tested in banking and SSC exams: Redundancy: Using "cannot" and "be able to" in the same clause is a "Superfluous Expression" error because both terms denote the same concept of ability. Double Negatives: Adverbs like hardly, scarcely, and barely already contain a negative sense. Using them with "cannot" or "can't" creates a grammatically incorrect double negative.

t: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
o: The committee has decided to postpone the meeting until next week.
The committee have decided to postpone the meeting until next week.
The committee is decided to postpone the meeting until next week.
The committee has been decided to postponing the meeting until next week.
e: Option a) is correct because "committee" is a singular collective noun, and the singular verb "has" agrees with it. Hence, option (a) is the answer. Option b) is incorrect because "have" is used for plural subjects, and "committee" is singular. Option c) is incorrect because "is decided" is grammatically incorrect; it should be "has decided." "Is decided" is the passive voice construction which does not fit in this sentence as the emphasis is on the doer of the action, the committee. Option d) is incorrect because "has been decided" implies a passive structure, which does not fit the context of the sentence. The emphasis is on the doer of the action, the committee. So, active voice construction would be appropriate. Note: Collective Noun: It is the name given to a number (or collection) of persons or things taken together and spoken of as one whole. Examples could be crowd, fleet, committee, family, army, jury, heard, etc. Voice of a sentence - Depending upon the emphasis we want to lay we use a particular voice in a particular context. We use active voice to lay emphasis on the doer of the action while we use passive voice to lay emphasis on the receiver of the action. Example: Active- Radha will work. (emphasis on Radha) Passive- Work will be done by Radha. (emphasis on Work)

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. He read a interesting book. The book was on history.
B. He read an interesting book. A book was on history.
C. He read an interesting book. The book was on history.
D. He read a interesting book. A book was on history.
e: Option A: Incorrect. 'A interesting' is incorrect because "interesting" begins with a vowel sound and requires 'an' as "an" is used before vowel-sounding words, while "a" is used before consonant-sounding words. The second sentence is correct, but cannot compensate for the first error. Option B: Incorrect. The first sentence is correct with 'an interesting', but the second sentence uses 'A book', which is inappropriate here. 'The book' (using the definite article "the") should be used to refer to the specific book mentioned earlier. Option C: Correct. Both sentences are correct. 'An interesting book' uses the correct article for a word beginning with a vowel sound, and 'the book' appropriately refers to the specific book previously mentioned. Option D: Incorrect. 'A interesting' is incorrect for the same reason as in Option A. The second sentence is also incorrect, as it uses 'A book' instead of 'The book'. Hence, option (d) is the answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
o: The poet and dramatist has been honored with the Sahitya Academy Award this year.
More than one student has successfully cleared the preliminary round of the exam.
Five miles are a long distance to cover on foot for an elderly person.
None of the information provided by the witness was found to be reliable.
e: The answer it Option (C)- as it remains the incorrect sentence. The plural verb "are" should be replaced with the singular verb "is." Rule 1 (The Primary Error): Units of Measurement When a plural noun (like miles, rupees, or liters) represents a specific distance, amount, or weight being treated as a single unit, the verb must be singular. Incorrect: Five miles are a long distance... Correct: Five miles is a long distance... Why the other sentences are CORRECT (The Traps) Why option (A) is correct: One Article Rule "The poet and dramatist" uses only one article ("The") before the first noun. This means one person is both a poet and a dramatist. Therefore, the singular verb "has" is perfectly correct. Why option (B) is correct: The "More than one" Rule Although "More than one" sounds plural, it is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb. "More than one student (singular) has (singular)..." is grammatically correct in formal English exams. Why Option (C) is Correct: The "None of" + Uncountable Rule In this sentence, "information" is an uncountable noun When "None of" is followed by an uncountable noun, the verb must be singular. Correct Sentence: Five miles is a long distance to cover on foot for an elderly person.

t: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
o: Two-thirds of the modern laboratory equipments were broken.
The variety of rare postage stamps were lost.
No worker and no senior clerk was present.
Most of the private digital information were leaked.
e: The Correct Ans is - Option (C)- This is the only sentence that adheres to the rules of Subject-Verb Agreement.Logic Breakdown:(A) Two-thirds of the modern laboratory equipments were broken:Error: The noun following "of" is "equipment," which is uncountable. Uncountable nouns (like water, milk, or equipment) always require a singular verb.Correction: ...equipment was broken.Equipment doesn’t take ‘s’.(B) The variety of rare postage stamps were lost:Error: The phrase "The variety of" focuses on the single group or selection. It must always take a singular verb. (Recall: "A variety" would take "were").Correction: The variety... was lost.(C) No worker and no senior clerk was present:Status: CORRECT. When two singular nouns are joined by "and" but are both preceded by the word "No," the subject is treated as singular (0 + 0 = 0). The singular verb "was" is perfectly correct.(D) Most of the private digital information were leaked:Error: The noun following "of" is "information," which is uncountable. Just like equipment, it cannot be pluralized and must take a singular verb.Correction: ...information was leaked.

t:
In the question given below, a sentence is given, divided into parts. One of the parts may contain an error. Identify the part that contains the error, and mark it as the answer. 
Govind avoids (A)/ to meet him (B)/ at his residence (C)/ in the evening (D).
e:
Part B has the error. The verbs enjoy, avoid, miss, postpone, and suggest are not followed by the to-infinitive. They should be used with the gerund.
The correct sentence is: Govind avoids meeting him at his residence in the evening.
Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

t:
Spot the error in the given sentence and select the sentence that is error free from the given options.
She is an ardent devotion.
e: In the given sentence, 'devotion' (love, loyalty, or enthusiasm for a person or activity) is incorrectly used instead of 'devotee' (a person who is very interested in and enthusiastic about someone or something) to denote a person. Option (b) has the same error as the given sentence. Option (a) lacks an auxiliary verb and in option (d), the adverb 'ardently' is used to qualify the noun 'devotee'. These options are erroneous and are thus negated. Option (c), 'She is an ardent devotee' is the grammatically and contextually correct sentence that can replace the given incorrect sentence. Hence, the correct answer is option (c). Note: Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'. Qualifiers: A word or phrase that limits the meaning of another word or phrase or makes it less general. 'Adverbs' and 'adjectives' are qualifiers.

t:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. Identify the part that has an error. Select the option that has an error.
<u>The supervisor was not pleased</u> about <u>him arriving late</u> to the <u> mandatory safety briefing</u> <u>for the third time</u> this month.
e: When a pronoun comes before a gerund (a verb ending in "-ing" that acts as a noun), the pronoun should be in the possessive case. The action the supervisor was not pleased about was the "arriving," so the pronoun should show possession of that action. So, the phrase "pleased about him arriving late" should be replaced with "pleased about his arriving late". Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t: Select the grammatically correct sentence. A) I have completed the initial draft of my novel. The editing process will start next week. B) I have complete the initial draft of my novel. The editing process will start next week. C) I have completes the initial draft of my novel. The editing process will start next week. D) I have completed the initial draft of my novel. The editing process will starts next week.
e: The grammatically correct sentence is A. The error in sentence B is related to verb form. The phrase "have complete" is incorrect because "complete" is the base form of the verb, whereas the present perfect tense requires the past participle form of the verb. The correct form is "have completed." The verb "complete" should be in the past participle form "completed" to match the present perfect tense of the sentence. The error in sentence C is again related to verb from. The phrase "have completes" is incorrect. The verb "completes" is in the present tense, but the present perfect tense requires the past participle form "completed." The error in sentence D is related to verb form. The phrase "will starts" is incorrect because "starts" is the present tense form, whereas "will" requires the base form of the verb. When using "will" for future tense, the verb that follows should be in its base form, not the third person singular form. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. NOTE: Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

t:
Identify the error in the given sentence and select the correct sentence from the given options.
This is the story of eight round planets, the few rocks in between, and some comets.
o: This is story of eight round planets, few rocks in between, and some comets.
This is a story of eight round planets, few rocks in between, and some comets.
This is the story of eight round planets, few rocks in between, and some comets.
This is the story of eight round planets, a few rocks in between, and some comets.
e:
The error in the original sentence lies in the phrase "the few rocks." In English, "few" without an article implies a small number but can sound incomplete or awkward in this context. The correct phrase is "a few rocks," which means a small number of rocks and is grammatically appropriate. Additionally, the original sentence is missing the article "a" before "story," but since the options focus on the phrase "few rocks," the correct choice addresses the primary error.
· Option 1 removes "the" before "story," making it incorrect ("This is story").
· Option 2 adds "a" before "story" but retains "few rocks," which is incorrect.
· Option 3 is identical to the original sentence, retaining the error.
· Option 4 corrects the phrase to "a few rocks," making it the correct choice.
Thus, the correct sentence is: This is the story of eight round planets, a few rocks in between, and some comets.

t:
Spot the erroneous part if any, in the following sentence. 
The success of the/ <u>project will depend for(A)/</u> effective communication/ <u>between team members(B)/</u> <u>and adherence to(C)/</u> the established timeline. / No error (D).
e:
The usual collocation for the word 'depend' is 'on' and not 'for'. Such an error is called prepositional mis-collocation error. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. 
The final sentence: The success of the project will depend on effective communication between team members and adherence to the established timeline.

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “what”: What the principal stated during the meeting surprised even the senior faculty members of the institution.
e: Answer: B) Relative Pronoun Explanation: A relative pronoun introduces a clause and connects it to the rest of the sentence. Words like who, which, that, and what can function as relative pronouns. Here, “what” introduces the clause: “What the principal stated during the meeting” This entire clause acts as the subject of the sentence. “What” also stands for “the thing which.” Therefore, it functions as a relative pronoun.

t: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
o: We must found a solution to this problem before it gets worse.
We must prioritises customer satisfaction in our business strategy.
They will start their journey early to avoid traffic.
He will called you as soon as he gets home from work.
e: The sentence given in option (c) is grammatically correct. This sentence uses the future tense ("will start") appropriately to indicate a future action. Option (a) is not correct. After the modal verb "must," we use the base form of the verb ("find"). But 'found' (past tense form) is not the base form. Modal verbs like "must" express necessity or obligation and are always followed by the base form of the main verb. So, 'found' should be replaced with the base form 'find'. The correct sentence is: We must find a solution to this problem before it gets worse. Option (b) is not correct. After the modal verb "must," we use the base form of the verb ("prioritise"). But 'prioritises' (present tense form) is not the base form. Modal verbs such as "must" indicate necessity and are followed by the base form of the verb that expresses the action required. So, 'prioritises' should be replaced with the base form 'prioritise'. The correct sentence is: We must prioritise customer satisfaction in our business strategy. Option (d) is incorrect as well. After the modal verb "will," we use the base form of the verb ("call"). Modal verbs like "will" express future actions or intentions and are followed by the base form of the main verb. But 'called' (past tense form) is not the base form. So, we should replace 'called' with the base form 'call'. The correct sentence is: He will call you as soon as he gets home from work. Hence, (c) is the correct answer. NOTE: Modal verb: A verb used with another verb to express an idea such as possibility that is not expressed by the main verb. The modal verbs in English are "can," "could," "may," "might," "must," "ought," "shall," "should," "will," and "would." They do not change their form (spelling) and they have no infinitive or participle (past/present). Example: I can speak Spanish. Here 'can' expresses the ability of the person to speak (main verb) Spanish. This ability cannot be expressed by the main verb 'speak'.

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “around”: The journalists gathered around the minister immediately after the conference ended.
e: Answer: A) Preposition Explanation: A preposition shows the relationship between a noun/pronoun and another word in the sentence. Here, “around” is followed by the noun phrase “the minister.” around the minister It shows position or direction in relation to the minister. Therefore, “around” functions as a preposition.

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Lest you will miss the flight, / you should leave for the / airport at least three hours early.
o: airport at least three hours early
Lest you will miss the flight,
e: The error is in the part "Lest you will miss the flight,". The conjunction 'lest' is used to express the intention of preventing something undesirable. It is always followed by the modal verb 'should'. Using 'will' or any other modal after 'lest' is grammatically incorrect. The correct pair is 'lest... should'. Correct Sentence: Lest you should miss the flight, you should leave for the airport at least three hours early. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: A conjunction (also called a connective) is a word such as and, because, but, for, if, or, when etc. Conjunctions are used to connect phrases, clauses, and sentences.

t:
Identify the error in the following sentence. 
She had beat all odds to achieve her long-cherished dream of becoming a successful entrepreneur.
e: The error in the sentence is in the word "beat." The correct past participle of "beat" in this context should be "beaten" instead of "beat." "Beat" is the present tense form, but in this sentence, we need the past participle form to convey the completed action in the past. The past participle of "beat" is "beaten." "Had", when acting as a helping verb, requires past participle after it. Therefore, the correction is necessary for grammatical accuracy. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. The corrected sentence would be: "She had beaten all odds to achieve her long-cherished dream of becoming a successful entrepreneur." Note: Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

t:
Spot the erroneous part if any, in the following sentence. 
The collection of/ <u>vintage coins were(A)/</u> meticulously curated, / <u>featuring rare pieces from(B)/</u> various historical periods/ <u>and regions around the world(C).</u> / No error (D).
e: The error here is related to subject-verb agreement. The subject of this sentence is "the collection," which is a singular noun. However, the verb used in this sentence is "were," which is the plural form of the verb "to be." This is incorrect because the subject "the collection" is singular, so the verb should also be singular. To correct this error, we should use the singular form of the verb "to be," which is "was". Hence, (a) is the correct answer. The final sentence: The collection of vintage coins was meticulously curated, featuring rare pieces from various historical periods and regions around the world. Note: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

t:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.
A. She bought a umbrella. It is an useful item during rainy season.
B. She bought an umbrella. It is a useful item during rainy season.
C. She bought a umbrella. It is a useful item during rainy season.
D. She bought an umbrella. It is an useful item during rainy season.
e: Option A: Incorrect. The indefinite article 'a' is incorrect because "umbrella" starts with a vowel sound, so 'an' should be used as "an" is used before vowel-sounding words, while "a" is used before consonant-sounding words. The second sentence also misuses 'an useful' because "useful" starts with a consonant sound, requiring 'a'. Option B: Correct. 'An umbrella' is correct because "umbrella" begins with a vowel sound. 'A useful item' is correct because "useful" begins with a consonant sound. Option C: Incorrect. The first sentence repeats the same error as in Option A by using 'a umbrella' instead of 'an umbrella'. The second sentence is correct. Option D: Incorrect. The first sentence is correct, but the second sentence repeats the error of using 'an useful' instead of 'a useful'. Hence, option (d) is the answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the bracketed segment in the given sentence.
We have felt strong tremors (in towards) state.
e:
The use of 'in' and 'towards' cannot be used together since they mean the same and thus avoid creating redundancy. Option (c), 'across the' is the most appropriate phrase to replace the phrase in the bracket ['across' means 'all over']. The rest of the options are grammatically incorrect. 'Inside' would be correct in place of 'side'; 'within' should replace 'with'; 'in' should replace 'into'.
The complete sentence is: We have felt strong tremors across the state.
Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. 
It is a well-known (A)/ fact that Sameer (B)/ visibly is leading (C)/ the team (D).
e:
Part C has an error. When the verb phrase has an auxiliary and a main verb, the adverb is placed between the auxiliary and the main verb. In this sentence, the adverb 'possibly' is placed before the auxiliary verb which is incorrect.
The correct sentence is: It is a well-known fact that Sameer is visibly leading the team.
Hence, the correct answer is option (b).

t:
Spot the error in the given sentence and select the correct sentence from the options given.
The infantry has taken the brunt of the missile attacks.
o: The infantry has been taken the brunt of the missile attacks.
The infantry have taken the brunt of the missile attacks.
The infantry is taking the brunt of the missile attacks.
The infantry was taken the brunt of the missile attacks.
e: 'Cattle, cavalry, poultry, children, gentry, infantry, police' are certain nouns that are singular in form but plural in meaning. They take plural verbs. The grammatically correct sentence is mentioned in option (b). 'Has, Is, and Was' are all plural verbs. The correct sentence is - 'The infantry have taken the brunt of the missile attacks.' Hence, option (b) is correct.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error. 
Samantha enjoys to spend weekends hiking in the mountains, finding solace and joy in the beauty of nature.
e: In segment (a), "enjoys to spend" is incorrect. After the verb "enjoys," the correct structure is to use the gerund form ("spending"), which acts as a noun and follows the verb. Therefore, "enjoys to spend" should be corrected to "enjoys spending" to maintain grammatical accuracy and clarity. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. Note: A gerund is a verb form that ends in "-ing" and functions as a noun in a sentence. The corrected sentence: Samantha enjoys spending weekends hiking in the mountains, finding solace and joy in the beauty of nature.

t:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an INCORRECT preposition.
Please remember to take / your notice to the reception area / if you want it to be displayed / upon the bulletin board.
o: if you want it to be displayed
your notice to the reception area
e:
Let's analyze each segment for the use of prepositions:
· Option 1: "Please remember to take" - This segment has no preposition, just the verb "take." It's grammatically correct as part of the sentence.
· Option 2: "upon the bulletin board" - The preposition "upon" is incorrect here. The standard preposition for displaying something on a bulletin board is "on," not "upon." "Upon" is more formal and typically used in different contexts (e.g., "upon arrival"). The correct phrase should be "on the bulletin board."
· Option 3: "if you want it to be displayed" - This segment has no preposition and is grammatically correct as a conditional clause.
· Option 4: "your notice to the reception area" - The preposition "to" is correct here, indicating the destination of the notice (i.e., "take your notice to the reception area").
The incorrect preposition is in Option 2, where "upon" should be replaced with "on."

t:
In the following sentence the underlined part contains an error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative.
The sky appeared to be <u>greyest</u> after the storm.
e:
The underlined word greyest is a superlative adjective, implying comparison among three or more items, which is not supported by the sentence context (no multiple items are compared). The sentence requires a simple adjective to describe the sky's appearance.
more grey: Comparative, implying comparison with another, not suitable without a specific comparison.
greyer: Comparative, also incorrect without a comparison.
most grey: Superlative, similar to "greyest," incorrect without multiple items.
grey: Base adjective, appropriate for a simple description: "The sky appeared to be grey after the storm."
Thus, grey is the correct alternative.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Economic analysts predict that if current growth rates persist, the emerging economy
will take over several developed nations in terms of total GDP output
within the next two decades, reshaping the global financial landscape entirely.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “take over” with “overtake”.📌 Rule / Concept: Overtake vs. Take overThese terms are frequently confused because they both involve a change in status or position, but their applications are distinct:Overtake: To catch up with and pass someone or something (physically, numerically, or in terms of progress). It is used for competition, speed, or growth (e.g., "The runner overtook his rival").Take over: To assume control, command, or possession of something. It is used for management, responsibilities, or business acquisitions (e.g., "The company was taken over by a giant corporation").💢 Application to the Given Question - In this context, the sentence refers to one economy growing faster and surpassing another in numerical value (GDP output). It does not mean the emerging economy is "assuming control" or "managing" the developed nations. Since it is a matter of surpassing a benchmark, overtake is the correct term.More Examples for Clarity - Example 1: Germany overtook Japan to become the world's third-largest economy.Example 2: The military decided to take over the government during the crisisExample 3: Don't let your emotions take over your sense of judgment.

t:
In the following question, a sentence is given which is divided into four parts. Out of the four parts, one part contains an error. Mark that option as your answer. 
More than one train have (A)/ been delayed due to (B)/ fog today, so you might (C)/ have to wait a little bit.
e:
Part A has an error. The phrases like 'more than one', 'many a' are singular in form but plural in meaning and take up singular verbs. So, 'have' should be replaced by 'has' in order to rectify the error. Hence, (b) is the correct answer. 
The final correct sentence would be: More than one train has been delayed due to fog today, so you might have to wait a little bit.

t:
Select the grammatically correct sentence. 

A. I need to do homework before going out to meet my friends.
B. I need to have homework before going out to meet my friends.
C. I need to done homework before going out to meet my friends.
D. I need to do homework before going out to meet mine friends.
e: Sentence A correctly uses the phrase "do homework" and is grammatically correct. The phrase "do homework" is appropriate for expressing the need to complete tasks. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. B- The phrase "have homework" suggests possessing or being assigned homework, rather than completing it, which is incorrect meaningfully. C- The phrase "to done" is incorrect. The correct form should be "to do", as the infinitive marker "to" should be followed by the base verb ['Done' is V2/V3]. D- The possessive pronoun "mine" is used without a following noun. Here, since the noun follows it, it should be replaced with "my" (possessive determiner). Note: Possessive Determiners/Adjectives: Words like 'my', 'our', 'your', 'his', 'her', 'its', and 'their' are known as possessive adjectives (or possessive determiners). They come before nouns and indicate ownership of the noun. Example: "The teacher asked the students to open their drawing books." Possessive Pronouns: The pronouns mine, yours, hers, his, ours, and theirs are known as possessive pronouns: they refer to something owned by the speaker or by someone or something previously mentioned. For example: The pen is mine. Infinitive marker: A word or affix attached to the stem of a verb in order to form the full infinitive. In English, to is the infinitive marker.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: The recruitment board finally declared that it is high time
the department increases the frequency of the
departmental examinations for the aspiring candidates.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (B). Replace “increases” with “increased”.Rule / Concept: Use V2 after ‘It is time/ It is high time/It is about time’ structure -The phrases "It is time," "It is high time," and "It is about time" are used to express that something should have happened in the past and is already delayed. When these phrases are followed by a Subject, the verb must be in the Simple Past Tense (V2).💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the phrase "it is high time" is followed by the subject "the department." Therefore, the following verb cannot be in the Simple Present (increases). It must be changed to the Simple Past form "increased" to correctly show that the increase in frequency is long overdue.

t:
Identify the segment in the sentence that contains a grammatical error. 
If I was you, I would consider taking some time off to recharge and reflect on what's important in life.
o: time off to recharge and reflect on
e: In segment (a), "was" is incorrect. The correct form to use in the subjunctive mood, expressing a hypothetical situation, is "were" with the first-person singular pronoun "I." The correct phrase should be "If I were you," indicating a hypothetical scenario where the speaker is imagining themselves in another person's position. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. The corrected sentence: If I were you, I would consider taking some time off to recharge and reflect on what's important in life.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: can finalize the design by Monday.
e: The Correct Answer is Option (c). 👉 Correction: Replace "can" with "could". The Core Rule: Tense Harmony- In English grammar, if the Principal Clause (the main part of the sentence) is in the Past Tense, the Subordinate Clause (the part starting with that, if, whether, etc.) must also be in the Past Tense. Rule: V2 (Main Clause)→V2 (Subordinate Clause) The Modal Shift: When moving into the past, present modals must shift to their past forms: Can becomes Could Will becomes Would May becomes Might

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: Given the volatile nature of the stock market this week,
the financial consultant suggested that the investors
had better to diversify their portfolios immediately.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “had better to diversify” with “had better diversify” 📌 Rule / Concept: The "Had Better" Construction The phrase "Had better" is a semi-modal idiom used to give advice, express a preference, or issue a warning. Despite the presence of the word "had" (which looks like past tense) and "better" (which looks like a comparison), it functions as a single unit meaning "should" or "ought to." The absolute rule for this idiom is that it must be followed by a Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to"). 💢 Application to the Given Question In lengthy, high-level questions, examiners surround the error with complex vocabulary like "volatile nature," "diversify," and "portfolios" to distract you from the simple verb pattern. "...investors had better to diversify their portfolios..." In the sentence above, the infinitive marker "to" has been incorrectly inserted before the verb "diversify." To correct the error, the "to" must be removed to satisfy the requirement of the bare infinitive. Corrected Sentence "Given the volatile nature of the stock market this week, the financial consultant suggested that the investors had better diversify their portfolios immediately."

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option.
Shyam and Dhyuti became parents (A)/ to daughter Raha in November; (B)/ he wants that Raha to look like Dhyuti (C)/ but not take her personality traits. (D)
e:
Part C has an error. 
The verb 'want' should not be used with a that-clause. It is used with the to-infinitive. So, the phrase 'wants that' is incorrect. 
The correct sentence is: Shyam and Dhyuti became parents to daughter Raha in November; he wants Raha to look like Dhyuti but not take her personality traits.
Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t:
In the question given below, a sentence is given, divided into parts. One of the parts may contain an error. Identify the part that contains the error, and mark it as the answer. 
Rony always stressed (A)/that one should (B)/ not to forget the (C)/person that helped one (D).
e:
Part C has the error. Infinitive without 'to' is also used after the verbs will, would, shall, should, may, might, can, could and must. In part C, 'to' is incorrectly placed before the verb 'forget'.
The correct sentence is: Rony always stressed that one should not forget the person that helped one.
Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

t: Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options. A. He found a hourglass. It was a unique discovery. B. He found an hourglass. It was an unique discovery. C. He found a hourglass. It was an unique discovery. D. He found an hourglass. It was a unique discovery.
e: Option A: Incorrect The word "hourglass" starts with a silent "h," making its sound begin with a vowel. Therefore, the indefinite article "a" is incorrect; it should be "an." The phrase "a unique discovery" is correct because "unique" begins with a consonant sound, which pairs correctly with "a." This is because "an" is used before vowel-sounding words, while "a" is used before consonant-sounding words. Option B: Incorrect The first sentence is correct as "hourglass" starts with a vowel sound, requiring "an." The article "an" in the second sentence is incorrect because "unique" starts with a consonant sound, so it should be preceded by "a." Option C: Incorrect As explained in Option A, "hourglass" requires "an," not "a." The second sentence is also incorrect, as "unique" shall be preceded by "a," not "an." Option D: Correct Correct use of the indefinite article "an" with "hourglass." Correct use of the indefinite article "a" with "unique." Hence, option (c) is the answer. Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o: While the marketing team successfully defended their strategy during the meeting, the creative
department insisted that the innovative concept for the upcoming digital campaign was
actually their and had been conceptualized during the previous quarter.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (C).Replace “their” with “theirs”Rule / Concept: Possessive Adjectives vs. Possessive PronounsPossessive Adjectives (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) must always be followed by a noun because they function as modifiers (e.g., their strategy). Possessive Pronouns (mine, ours, yours, his, hers, its, theirs) stand alone and replace the "Possessive Adjective + Noun" structure to avoid repetition. They never take a noun after them.NOTE: POSSESSIVE PRONOUN = POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE + NOUNExample: yours = your + dog (noun)Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, there is no noun following the word "their." Since the sentence is referring to "the creative department's concept" without repeating the word "concept," a possessive pronoun is required. "Their" is an adjective and cannot stand alone; "theirs" is the correct pronoun.Things to Remember / Exam Tips-The Noun Check: Always look at what follows the word. If there is a noun (e.g., their house), use the adjective. If there is a verb or a full stop (e.g., is theirs.), use the pronoun.-The "s" Factor: Except for "mine," most possessive pronouns end in "s" (ours, yours, hers, theirs).-Avoid the Apostrophe: Never use an apostrophe with possessive pronouns (theirs, NOT their's).

t:
Three segments of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. One of them may contain an error. Select the option that contains the error. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
<u>When my father will come</u>, <u>I will make sure</u> that <u>I discuss the possibilities</u> of a new business venture with him.
e:
The error is in the segment "When my father will come." In English, the simple present tense is used in "when" clauses for future events, not the future tense "will." The correct form is "When my father comes." 
The corrected sentence is: "When my father comes, I will make sure that I discuss the possibilities of a new business venture with him."
Option a: I will make sure - Correct, as it uses the future tense appropriately.
Option b: No error - Incorrect, as there is a clear error in option c.
Option d: I discuss the possibilities - Correct in the context of the subjunctive mood after "make sure that."
Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The manager made the new intern / to stay back after office hours / to finish the urgent report.
o: to stay back after office hours
The manager made the new intern
e: The error is in the part "to stay back after office hours". Certain verbs like 'make', 'let', 'help', and 'bid', when used in the active voice, are followed by a bare infinitive (the base form of a verb without 'to'). In this sentence, 'made' is used in the active voice. Therefore, the infinitive marker 'to' should be removed before the verb 'stay'. The correct phrase is "stay back". Correct Sentence: The manager made the new intern stay back after office hours to finish the urgent report. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Note: · Infinitive: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, often preceded by to. Consider the sentences given below: · To err is human. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to err' is the subject of the verb 'is'] · My father likes to cook. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to cook' is the object of the verb 'likes'] · To vote in elections is our right. [the infinitive 'to vote', like a noun, is the subject of the verb 'is', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (elections)] · Radha went to the lake to fetch water. [the infinitive 'to fetch', like a noun, is the object of the verb 'went', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (water)] · The above sentences illustrate various ways in which infinitives are used. It can both act as a noun and a verb. · Infinitive marker: A word or affix attached to the stem of a verb in order to form the full infinitive. In English, to is the infinitive marker. · Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).

t:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The new investigative committee comprised of / ten senior officers who were / experts in forensic science.
o: The new investigative committee comprised of
e: The error is in the part "The new investigative committee comprised of". The verb 'comprise' means 'to consist of' or 'to be made up of'. In the active voice, 'comprise' is not followed by the preposition 'of'. The preposition 'of' is used when the sentence is in the passive voice (e.g., 'was comprised of'). The preposition 'of' should be removed to make the sentence grammatically correct in the active voice. Alternatively, 'comprised of' could be replaced with 'consisted of'. Correct Sentence: The new investigative committee comprised ten senior officers who were experts in forensic science. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. Note: · Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice.
