e: The Correct Ans is - Option (A)The singular verb "has" is the only correct choice to match the uncountable subject.Rule/Concept: "Some of" with Uncountable Nouns The words Some of, Most of, and All of are "transparent." The verb ignores these words and agrees strictly with the noun that follows the preposition "of".The Subject: The noun after "of" is "evidence."The Property: "Evidence" is an uncountable noun. In English grammar, uncountable nouns are always singular and never take a plural verb, even if they refer to a large collection of items.Logic BreakdownThe Distractor: The sentence includes plural nouns like "scenes" and "vehicles" right before the blank. These are placed there to trick your ear into choosing the plural options (B, C, or D).Correct Sentence: Some of the forensic evidence recovered from the primary crime scenes and the multiple suspects' vehicles has been sent to the laboratory...

t: Select a grammatically correct sentence using the future tense.
o: As soon as the sun will set, the streetlights will turn on automatically.
As soon as the sun sets, the streetlights will turn on automatically.
As soon as the sun will set, the streetlights are turning on automatically.
As soon as the sun has set, the streetlights would turn on automatically.
e: The correct option is b) As soon as the sun sets, the streetlights will turn on automatically. This sentence demonstrates the correct structure for future time clauses. When a clause begins with a time conjunction like "as soon as," "when," "before," or "after" and refers to the future, it must use the simple present tense ("sets"). The main clause then uses the simple future tense ("will turn on"). Let's look at why the other options are incorrect: · Option (a): This is incorrect because the future tense ("will set") cannot be used in a future time clause starting with "as soon as". · Option (c): This has two errors: it incorrectly uses the future tense in the time clause and uses the present continuous tense ("are turning on") in the main clause, which is less appropriate than the simple future for a statement of future fact. · Option (d): This has two errors: it incorrectly uses the present perfect ("has set") in the time clause and "would" instead of "will" in the main clause.

t: The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar."The jury, having reached a unanimous agreement after several days of intense deliberation, _________ now delivering its final verdict to the presiding judge."
e: The Correct Ans is - Option (A).The singular verb "is" is required because the jury is acting as a single, unified body.Rule/Concept: Collective Nouns as a Unit When a collective noun (Jury, Committee, Team) acts as a single unit or reaches a unanimous decision, it is treated as Singular.The Clue: The word "unanimous" and the singular pronoun "its" indicate that the group is acting as one entity.Logic Breakdown:The Subject: "The jury" is the collective noun.The Action: "Delivering its final verdict" shows that the entire group is doing one single thing at the same time.The Choice: Since the action is unified, the verb must be the singular "is." Correct Sentence: The jury... is now delivering its final verdict...

t: In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “despite”: Despite receiving repeated warnings from the committee, the contractor continued using substandard materials during the construction of the bridge.
e: Answer: C) Preposition Explanation: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship of a noun or pronoun with another word in the sentence. Prepositions are usually followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund (-ing form). Here, “despite” is followed by the phrase “receiving repeated warnings.” It shows contrast between the warnings and the contractor’s actions. Therefore, “despite” functions as a preposition.

t: The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar. Had the investigators arrived at the crime scene a few minutes earlier, they _________ have caught the perpetrators before they escaped through the back alley.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (b). Rule/Concept: Might (Remote Possibility in Conditionals) - 'Might' is used to express a very weak or remote possibility. In the context of Conditional Type 3 (past unreal situations), we use the structure: If + Subject + had + V3, Subject + might + have + V3. Application to the Given Question - The sentence uses an inverted conditional structure ("Had the investigators arrived" instead of "If the investigators had arrived"). It describes a past possibility that did not happen. 'Might' correctly fits the "remote possibility" required by the context of a near-miss at a crime scene. More Examples for Clarity- If I had worked harder, I might have passed the exam. (Possibility) If it had rained, the match might have been cancelled. (Remote chance) Things to Remember / Exam Tips- Remote vs. Strong: Use 'May' for a 50% chance and 'Might' for a 20-30% chance. Inversion Trap: "Had + Subject + V3" is just a formal way of writing "If + Subject + had + V3". Don't let the lack of "If" confuse you. Past Tense of May: In Indirect Speech, 'May' always changes to 'Might'. (e.g., He said that it might rain).

t: The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar. In accordance with the ethical guidelines of journalism, a reporter _________ verify the authenticity of a lead from at least two independent sources before publishing it.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (a). Rule / Concept: Ought to (Moral Duty and Correctness)- Ought to is a modal verb used to express a moral obligation, duty, or the "correct" thing to do according to a standard or ethical code. It is structurally unique among modals because it must be followed by the to-infinitive (to + V1). While 'should' also expresses duty, 'ought to' is preferred when referring to laws, regulations, or established social ethics. Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the context is "ethical guidelines of journalism." This refers to a professional moral code. Since the blank is followed by the base form "verify," we need a modal. Why not "Should"? While "should" is logically similar, in many competitive exams, when a sentence refers to "Ethical Guidelines," "Fundamental Duties," or "Constitutional Values," 'Ought to' is the more precise choice to reflect a formal moral obligation. More Examples for Clarity You ought to respect your elders. (Moral Duty) ✔ We ought to follow the traffic rules for everyone's safety. (Social Obligation) ✔ This film ought to win an award for its screenplay. (Strong Desirability) ✔ Incorrect Usage We should to help the poor. (Never use 'to' with should) ❌ You ought respect your parents. (Missing 'to') ❌

t: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
o: The committee of senior executives, after weeks of deliberation over the proposed merger, have finally released its unanimous decision to the eagerly waiting public and media.
The committee of senior executives, after weeks of deliberation over the proposed merger, has finally released their unanimous decision to the eagerly waiting public and media.
The committee of senior executives, after weeks of deliberation over the proposed merger, have finally released their unanimous decision to the eagerly waiting public and media.
The committee of senior executives, after weeks of deliberation over the proposed merger, has finally released its unanimous decision to the eagerly waiting public and media.
e: This question tests subject-verb agreement with a collective noun. A collective noun ("committee") takes a singular verb when it acts as a single, cohesive unit. The word "unanimous" confirms that the committee is acting as one body. · Subject: "The committee" (acting as a singular unit). · Verb: Must be singular ("has"). · Possessive Determiner: Must also be singular ("its") to be consistent. Let's analyze the options: · a) This sentence incorrectly uses a plural verb ("have") with a singular pronoun ("its"). This is a mismatch. · b) This sentence correctly uses a singular verb ("has") but incorrectly uses a plural pronoun ("their"). The pronoun must also be singular. · c) This sentence incorrectly uses both a plural verb ("have") and a plural pronoun ("their"). Since the committee is unanimous, it should be treated as singular. · d) This sentence is perfectly correct. It uses the singular verb "has" to agree with the united "committee," and the singular possessive pronoun "its" is consistent with this singular treatment. The correct sentence is: The committee of senior executives, after weeks of deliberation over the proposed merger, has finally released its unanimous decision to the eagerly waiting public and media. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

t: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
o: What truly defines success in this competitive field are not just technical skill but also the unwavering determination and resilience to overcome inevitable failures.
What truly defines success in this competitive field is not just technical skill but also the unwavering determination and resilience to overcome inevitable failures.
What truly define success in this competitive field is not just technical skill but also the unwavering determination and resilience to overcome inevitable failures.
What truly define success in this competitive field are not just technical skill but also the unwavering determination and resilience to overcome inevitable failures.
e: This question tests subject-verb agreement where the subject of the sentence is a noun clause beginning with "What." The formal and most widely accepted rule is that a noun clause serving as a subject is treated as singular and takes a singular verb, regardless of whether the subject complement is singular or plural. · Subject: The entire clause "What truly defines success in this competitive field." This clause represents a single concept or idea, so it is grammatically singular. · Verb in the Clause: The subject of the inner clause is "What," which takes the singular verb "defines." · Main Verb: The main verb must agree with the singular noun clause subject. Therefore, it must be singular ("is"). Let's analyze the options: · a) The main verb "are" is plural and incorrect. It should be "is" to agree with the singular "What" clause. · b) This sentence is perfectly correct. The verb in the clause "defines" is singular. The main verb "is" is also singular, correctly agreeing with the singular noun clause subject. · c) The verb in the clause "define" is plural and incorrect. The main verb "is" is correct. · d) Both verbs are incorrect. "define" should be "defines," and "are" should be "is." The correct sentence is: What truly defines success in this competitive field is not just technical skill but also the unwavering determination and resilience to overcome inevitable failures. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

t:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the bracketed segment in the given sentence.
The team (has win) several awards for their innovative work.
e: In the sentence, 'has' indicates a present perfect tense, which is used to describe actions that started in the past and continue into the present or have just been completed. In the present perfect tense, the auxiliary verb "has" is used with the past participle form of the main verb. But 'win' (base form) is not the past participle form. For irregular verbs like "win", the past participle form is "won". Therefore, the correct structure is "has won" (option a). Options (b) and (d) are not correct. In present perfect tenses, after "has" or "have", we use the past participle form of the verb, not the present participle form "winning". Option (c) is also incorrect. 'Had' indicates a past perfect tense. The past perfect tense is formed using the auxiliary verb "had" plus the past participle of the main verb. But 'win' (base form) is not the past participle form. Hence, (a) is the correct answer. The correct sentence is: The team has won several awards for their innovative work. NOTE: "Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective." Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'. Irregular verbs: Irregular verbs are verbs that do not follow the standard pattern of conjugation in the past tense and past participle forms. In English, most verbs are regular, meaning they form their past tense and past participle by adding -ed to the base form (e.g., walk becomes walked). However, irregular verbs have unique forms that must be memorized because they do not follow this pattern. For example: go-went-gone, eat-ate-eaten, win-won-won, etc.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. 
In many ways, she (A)/ was a reluctant heroine of the Mutiny, (B)/ whom happened to be at (C)/ the wrong place at the right time. (D)
e:
Part C has an error.
In the given sentence, 'she' is the subject of the sentence. The relative pronoun 'whom' refers to the object of a sentence. So, its use is grammatically incorrect in the given sentence. 'Whom' should be replaced with the relative pronoun 'who' to rectify the given sentence. 'Who' is used to refer to the subject of a sentence. 
Hence, option (c) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: In many ways, she was a reluctant heroine of the Mutiny, who happened to be at the wrong place at the right time.

t:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option.
The United Nations has (A)/ declared Finland as (B)/ a world's happiest nation (C)/ for the third consecutive year. (D)
e:
Part C has an error. 
'Happiest' is a superlative degree adjective. We always use the definitive article 'the' with a superlative degree adjective. So, the indefinite article 'a' should be replaced with the definite article 'the' to rectify the given sentence. 
Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. 
The correct sentence is: The United Nations has declared Finland as the world's happiest nation for the third consecutive year.

t: The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar. The financial analyst clarified that since the company has already surpassed its quarterly revenue targets, the board _________ not authorize any additional emergency funding.
e: The Correct Ans is Option (b). Rule / Concept: Need as a Semi-Modal (Negative Usage)- When "Need" acts as a modal verb (marginal auxiliary), it is primarily used in negative sentences and questions. In this modal form, it follows two strict rules: It does not take 's' even with third-person singular subjects (He, She, It, The Board). It is followed by the Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to"). Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "need" is followed by "not" and the base verb "authorize." Here, "need" is acting as a modal. Even though the subject "The board" is singular, we cannot use "needs" because in the presence of "not" (acting as a modal), the 's' is dropped. Option (a) "needs" would only be correct if it were a main verb (e.g., The board needs to authorize...). Correct Usage - He need not go there. (Modal usage) Need I speak to him? (Interrogative modal usage) She needs to go there. (Main verb usage - 's' and 'to' included) Incorrect Usage He needs not go there. (Incorrect modal form) ❌ She need not to cry. (Never use 'to' after modal 'need') ❌ Things to Remember / Exam Tips The 'S' & 'To' Rule: If there is a NOT after need, do not use 's' and do not use 'to'. Subject-Verb Neutrality: As a modal, 'need' is like 'can' or 'must'—it never changes its form based on the subject. Main Verb vs. Modal: Modal: Subject + need + not + V1 Main Verb: Subject + does/do + not + need + to + V1

A) 'was'के बदले 'were' का प्रयोग होगा क्योंकि यदि वाक्य का Subject 'Many, Both, Few, A few' हो तो Verb Plural होता है; जैसे— 
 (i) Both are happy. 
 (ii) Many were invited but a few have come. 
 इसलिए, सही वाक्य होगा — 'Many of the participants were eager to share their experiences during the workshop session held at the university auditorium.' 
 (i) Both are happy. 
 (ii) Many were invited but a few have come. 
 Therefore, the correct sentence would be — 'Many of the participants were eager to share their experiences during the workshop session held at the university auditorium.'

e:
D) 'have'के बदले 'has' का प्रयोग होगा क्योंकि 'More than one' के बाद Singular Noun और Singular Verb होता है; जैसे— 
 (i) More than one room is vacant. 
 किंतु, यदि 'More + Plural Noun + than one' का प्रयोग हो, तो Verb Plural होता है; जैसे— 
 (i) More teachers than one are late. 
 इसलिए, सही वाक्य होगा — 'More than one student has expressed their willingness to participate in the research project that aims to explore innovative solutions to climate change.' 
 (i) More than one room is vacant. 
 However, if the structure is 'More + Plural Noun + than one,' then the Verb is Plural; like— 
 (i) More teachers than one are late. 
 Therefore, the correct sentence would be — 'More than one student has expressed their willingness to participate in the research project that aims to explore innovative solutions to climate change.'

 'the higher you go' will be used instead of 'higher you go from' because this is a comparative structure where 'the higher...the colder' is used to show increasing degrees of comparison. Such structures are used to indicate proportional comparisons; Like— The higher you go, the colder it gets.

to bring in two ordinances on food contamination,

 'divert' will be used instead of 'diverts' because with 'cannot' we always use the Base Form (V1) of the verb. 'Diverts' is in the Simple Present (V5), which is incorrect here. The correct word is 'divert'; like— The new rules cannot divert attention from the actual problem.

 'who' will be used instead of 'whom' because 'who' is a subject pronoun, whereas 'whom' is used as an object pronoun. In this case, 'Rafael Nadal' is the subject, so 'who' is appropriate; Like— "She is the one who made the decision."

 Instead of 'will have been worked,' the correct form is'will have been working,' as the sentence is in the Future Perfect Continuous Tense. This tense is used to indicate an action that will continue for a period of time up to a certain point in the future. The use of "worked" (past participle) is incorrect here because it indicates Passive Voice, which is not suitable in this context. 
 Example: Mahesh and his workers will have been working on the project for a long time.

 'created among people' will be used instead of 'created between people' because 'among' is used when referring to relationships involving three or more people or things, whereas 'between' is used for relationships involving only two; Like— There is a sense of camaraderie among the members of the team.

t:
Parts of following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
<u>Has</u> Gita <u>an</u>y previous knowledge of <u>work</u> <u>with</u> junior colleagues?
e: When prepositions ['of' in the given sentence] are followed by the verb, the verb should in present participle [-ing] form. So, 'work' should be replaced with 'working'. 'Work' acts as a noun as well, but in the given sentence it is a verb as previous knowledge of an action of working with the junior colleagues is being discussed. Hence, option (d) is the answer. Note: A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples I. The teacher scolded the child for being late. II. We're going to a party. · The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition. · The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

t:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. One of them contains an error. The underlined parts are given as options with some changes. Select the option that correctly rectifies the error.
<u>Raveena's daughter</u> Kavya is <u>most intelligent</u> student and <u>she consistently</u> achieves <u>top grades</u>.
e:
The phrase "most intelligent student" lacks the definite article 'the'. It should be "the most intelligent student" or "an intelligent student." Option (c) corrects this by providing the phrase "an intelligent."
Option a: Incorrect. "Raveenas' daughter" introduces a spelling error (apostrophe misuse) and doesn't fix the article issue.
Option b: Incorrect. "She has consistently" changes the verb tense unnecessarily and doesn't address the article error.
Option d: Incorrect. "Topper grades" is not idiomatic; "top grades" is correct as is.
The correct sentence is: Raveena's daughter Kavya is an intelligent student, and she consistently achieves top grades.
Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. One of them contains an error. The underlined parts are given as options with some changes. Select the option that correctly rectifies the error.
The <u>film received</u> critical <u>acclaim for</u> being <u>a more innovative</u> movie <u>of the year</u>.
e:
The error is in the phrase "a more innovative." The adverb 'more' can be used when two things are in comparison. In the given sentence talks about one specific movie for which comparison is not required and the correct phrase to replace this is 'an innovative'.
The correct sentence: The film received critical acclaim for being an innovative movie of the year.
Hence, the correct answer is option (d).

It was <u>the home minister</u> of the country who took the decision to change <u>a laws pertaining</u> to <u>migration</u> of people from one state to another.
e:
The error is in "a laws"; "laws" is plural, so it should be "the laws" or "laws" without an article. "The laws pertaining" corrects this.
No error: There is an error in "a laws," so this is incorrect.
The migration: This part is correct; "migration" is appropriately used.
An home minister: This would be incorrect if it were in the sentence, but the original has "the home minister," which is correct.
The correct sentence: It was the home minister of the country who took the decision to change the laws pertaining to migration of people from one state to another.
Hence, the correct answer is option (b).

e: The correct verb tense should align with the past context of the sentence ("argued"). The art historian's argument is in the past, so "was greatly underestimated" would be more appropriate than "has been," which implies a present perfect tense. t: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. "Though the / global financial crisis, / China's economy continues / to grow at an impressive rate."
o: To grow at an impressive rate
e: "Though" must be followed by a complete clause (subject + verb). The correct preposition here is "Despite" (के बावजूद), which can directly precede a noun phrase.

t: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. "Mr. Unkerton glanced / to the inspector, / who merely snorted / and looked at the ceiling."
e: The verb "glanced" takes the preposition "at," not "to." The correct phrase is "glanced at the inspector."

t: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. "Since 1988, / the people of Rajasthan / have been searching / for 25-year-old man."
e: A singular countable noun requires an article. The correct phrase is "for a 25-year-old man."

t: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. "(a) The more it rains, / (b) worse / (c) the roads become / (d) No error"
e: In comparative correlative constructions ("the more..."), the corresponding part must also include "the." It should be "the worse."

t: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. "The compensation that the / Government agreed to provide to / the dependents of the / train accident is fairly less."
e: People cannot be dependents of an "accident". The correct, logical phrase is "the dependents of the train accident victims."

t: Identify the segment that contains an error. "One of the great rivers / of China, a Hwang Ho, / originates from the / eastern face of Tibet."
e: "Hwang Ho" is a proper noun (name of a river). Proper nouns do not require an indefinite article ("a"). It should just be "Hwang Ho."

And hear what he has to say
